events.text: Elder Beopjin has you kneel where the bell rope comes down through the roof. "Take no life you could spare," the old monk says. "Keep nothing you do not need. People think the first is the hard one." The rope sways a little, with nobody touching it. The novice behind you has stopped breathing to listen.

choices.text: Say it, and put your hand on the rope

effects.log: You say it. The bell does not ring, which the elder seems to think is correct. In the morning your bowl is set out one place further up the row, and nobody mentions it.

choices.text: Ask what happens to those who cannot

effects.log: Beopjin considers you. "They come back," the elder says. "Most of the people in this hall came back." It is not the answer you wanted, and you swear anyway.

events.text: Old Yeon Cheol takes you to a stream and tells you to swear to it. "It has held no office in ten thousand years," the old teacher says, "and it has worn through that mountain. Yield, then overcome. No seat of power. Say it to the water, it is the only one who will remember." A goat watches from the far bank with no opinion.

choices.text: Say it to the water

effects.log: You say it, and feel a little foolish, and the water goes on. By the time you reach the path you have stopped feeling foolish. You could not say when.

choices.text: Say it to the goat, since it is listening

effects.log: Yeon Cheol laughs until he has to sit down on a rock. "Good," he says. "That one holds no office either." The vow takes all the same.

events.text: Registrar Gu lays out the book, the brush and a very small cup of tea. "Serve. Keep your name clean of the law. Write nothing you would not sign." The registrar turns the book toward you. Forty years of signatures run down the page, and three of them have been ruled through, in red, in the same hand as the rest.

choices.text: Sign under the last name

effects.log: You sign. The registrar blots it, reads it, and blots it again. "Your hand slopes when you are nervous," the registrar says. "That will be noted, and it will be kept."

choices.text: Ask about the three ruled through

effects.log: "One took a bribe. One told a lie to a court. One was me," the registrar says, and pours the tea. "It can be come back from. It takes about nine years." You sign.

events.text: Old Banner Cheon carries the flag out himself, though it takes him a long time now. The cloth has more darns than cloth. "Never leave a friend," he says. "Bow to no wickedness. This has been through nine fights and we lost six of them, and nobody who stood under it has ever said they were sorry." He holds out the hem.

choices.text: Take the hem in both hands, and say it

effects.log: It smells of smoke and old rain. You say it loud enough for the yard, because you are fairly sure that is the point. Someone at the back starts a very bad song.

choices.text: Ask which of the six he remembers best

effects.log: He names the worst of them, and every person who was standing beside him. It takes a while. Then he holds out the hem again, and you take it.

events.text: Toll-Mother Gang has you up on the roof of the stronghold, where you can see every road that pays her. "The strong eat," she says, chewing. "No leash from anyone weaker than you. It is short, because the last one who wrote it down could only count to two." She spits over the wall, and holds out her knife, handle first, to see what you do.

choices.text: Take the knife, and say it back to her

effects.log: You say it back, and hand her the knife back too. She looks at you for a while. "Hm," she says, and it is the warmest thing anyone has said to you up here.

choices.text: Leave the knife, and say it anyway

effects.log: She laughs with all the teeth she has left. "That one will either run this place or be buried under it," she tells the wall, and goes back to her chewing.

events.text: Aunt Dok makes you drink something first. It is only after it is down that she tells you it was harmless, and that you should remember how that felt. "Every poison has its cure. Never turn on a guest at your own fire. People join us for the first half of that." Her hands, you notice, have no skin left on the fingertips.

choices.text: Swear with the taste still in your mouth

effects.log: You swear. She nods and gives you something to take the taste away, and that one, she says, was not harmless at all. You spend a thoughtful evening.

choices.text: Ask her what the cure was

effects.log: "There wasn't one. It was barley water," she says. "That is the first lesson, and you got it for free." You swear before she can think of a second.

events.text: Lamp Elder Mok unrolls the oath, written in red ink so old it has gone brown. "Nothing is owed to the weak. Do not go soft." The elder taps the page. "You will meet people who say this makes you a monster. They will mostly be people you have something they want." The lamp burns very straight in a room with four open windows.

choices.text: Sign in the red ink

effects.log: The brush is heavier than a brush should be. Nobody congratulates you. In the morning a junior you have never met steps out of your way on the stairs, and does not look up.

choices.text: Ask the elder whether going soft is really the worst of it

effects.log: Mok looks at you for some time. "It is the worst thing that can happen to you here," the elder says. "I said nothing about elsewhere." You sign.

events.text: Ledger Sister Ran opens the book of the Ancestor to a clean page and writes your name at the top. "Every breath is on loan," she says, without looking up. "You will be told what is owed. Do not go soft, and do not fall behind." Above your name, the page before has been closed and tied with red cord. She does not say whose it was.

choices.text: Put your thumb to the page

effects.log: Only ink. She looks almost disappointed. "The old way was messier," she says. "This one holds just as well." You carry the page in your head from then on, every day.

choices.text: Ask who the last page belonged to

effects.log: "Someone who asked," she says, and turns the book toward you. You put your thumb to the page.

events.text: You stand in your own hall, and it is Headwoman Ahn of the village below who has come up to hear it, because you asked her to. "The people before the sect," she repeats, doubtfully. "No one turned away hungry. That is a great many mouths." Half your disciples are trying not to look worried about the rice.

choices.text: Say it, in front of all of them

effects.log: You say it. Ahn nods as she might to a promising calf. By next week there is a line at your gate, because she has told everyone, as you knew she would.

choices.text: Ask her to say what she would hold you to

effects.log: She has it ready: the two bad bridges, the well, the tax. You write it on the wall under the creed. It is the least poetic oath in the murim, and it may be the heaviest.

events.text: Comptroller Sim has drawn up your oath as a contract, in three copies. "Everything is paid for. Every debt is written down. It is binding on you, and, I would point out, on anyone who owes you." The ink is good. So is the paper. You notice that the penalty clause has been left for you to fill in yourself.

choices.text: Fill in the penalty, and sign

effects.log: You write something that makes Sim's eyebrows move a very little, which from Sim is a standing ovation. All three copies go into three different vaults.

choices.text: Ask Sim what most people write

effects.log: "Too little," says Sim. "And then they pay it, and go on as before." You write down rather more than that, and sign.

events.text: List-Keeper Gyo brings the book to your hall in a box, and the first page has only a few names on it, in your own hand, from a long time ago. "No wrong goes unwritten. None forgiven for nothing." The keeper sharpens a pen that does not need it. "The second part is the one people miss. You may forgive. It simply has to cost them."

choices.text: Swear on the first name

effects.log: You lay your palm on the first name and swear. It is a smaller thing than you once imagined, and it holds a good deal better for that.

choices.text: Add a name before you swear

effects.log: You write one more, and Gyo reads it upside down without comment. The keeper has clearly been expecting it for some years. Then you swear.

events.text: Your first step is an alms bowl and the road to Sooncheon. Beg for a month, Elder Beopjin says, and bring back what you have left. In the second week, a boy named Tan follows you, a novice who has run away, with a hungry look and no shoes. Your bowl has three days of rice in it. He has not asked for any. He has simply started to walk beside you.

choices.text: Talk him through why he ran, on the road, and let him choose

ok.log: He talks for two days. On the third he turns round by himself, and takes half your rice for the walk. You come back to the temple with an empty bowl and no account to give of it. Beopjin looks in the bowl for a while and nods.

fail.log: You talk well, and he hears none of it. He vanishes one night with the rice, and you come back with an empty bowl and a sore conscience. "That is not the same empty," Beopjin says. Next year.

choices.text: Give him the bowl itself, and go on begging with your hands

effects.log: You beg with your hands for the rest of the month, which is every bit as bad as it sounds. Beopjin looks at your hands, and passes you without asking anything.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: The second step is the Hall of the Empty Bowl, where you must sit until you have stopped wanting anything. Nobody checks. There is no door. On the ninth day a man you once beat in a fight is brought in to sit next to you, and he smells of his own fear. He has come to apologise, which is somehow much worse.

choices.text: Hear him out, and find out what you actually feel

ok.log: What you feel turns out to be mostly tired. You tell him so. He weeps a little, and you find that you have stopped keeping score, and you did not notice the moment it happened.

fail.log: You hear him out, and feel very holy about it, and that is the trouble. On the fortieth day you admit this to Beopjin. "Yes," the elder says. "We could smell it." Another year.

choices.text: Stay in the hall until he has gone, however long that is

effects.log: He stays forty days. So do you. You come out thin, and quiet, and nobody says you have passed, and your bowl moves up the row.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last step is a fight, and nobody warned you. Three bandits have come to the temple gate with torches, and the abbot has sent word: they are to go home alive, with nothing broken, and you are to see to it alone. The novices are lined along the wall to watch. Tan is among them, in shoes now. Someone has already started to pray for the bandits.

choices.text: Take all three, and hurt none of them

ok.log: It takes most of the night. They go home at dawn with sore wrists and no torches, and one comes back within the year with his head shaved. The elder rings the bell, once, for the first time you have ever heard it.

fail.log: One of them falls badly, and he will limp. Nobody blames you. You do. "You could have spared that," Beopjin says, and it is not a reproach, only a measurement. Another year.

choices.text: Stand in the gate, and let them hit you until they stop

effects.log: They are surprised by how long it takes. In the end the eldest of them sits down and starts to cry. You are carried in, and the bell rings once, over your head, for the first time you have ever heard it.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Old Yeon Cheol sends you up the back of the mountain to learn from a master who lives there. It turns out to be Ji, a goatherd of about twelve, who has never heard of qi. For a month you follow the goats. They do not go up anywhere directly. You have started to notice this, and you are beginning to resent it.

choices.text: Stop climbing, and go where the goats go

ok.log: You reach the top in the same time as you would have, and rather less tired. Ji is unimpressed, having known this already. Yeon Cheol asks you what you learned, and you say "goats," and that seems to be correct.

fail.log: You go straight up, to prove something. You prove it, at some length, with a twisted ankle, and Ji brings you down on a goat. Next year, says Yeon Cheol, trying very hard not to enjoy this.

choices.text: Sit on a rock until a goat tells you otherwise

effects.log: It takes eleven days. Nothing happens, and then you notice that you are no longer waiting. You come down with burrs in your robe, and you are passed.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: The stream at the temple has run dry, and the elders ask you to bring it back. Everyone knows how: there is a landslide up the valley, a day's work for someone at your level. Yeon Cheol watches you sharpen your will and says nothing. Halfway up you find the slide has made a small new pool, and there are herons in it who have clearly just moved in.

choices.text: Leave it, and find where the water wants to go now

ok.log: It wants to go round by the east terrace, as it turns out, and it needs one stone moved. The temple has a new stream and the herons keep their pool. The elders mention your name once, in passing, which is the highest honour they have.

fail.log: You move the wrong stone. Half the east terrace is now a marsh, and you spend the season helping to dig it out. The herons do not seem to mind. Next year.

choices.text: Dig a channel by hand, one basket at a time

effects.log: It takes all summer. The herons get used to you. By the end you could not say what your own strength was for. You are passed, and you do not much notice.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last step is a duel on the Terrace of Clouds against a sword from the capital who has come to make his name. He is very good and he knows it. The whole sect watches. Your orders from Yeon Cheol are short: "Do not win." The challenger bows. You have the distinct feeling that you are also not supposed to lose.

choices.text: Give him nothing to hit, until he stops

ok.log: For an hour he strikes at where you were. Then he lowers his sword and stands breathing, and looks at it, and then at you. He asks to stay, and you find yourself showing him to the guest room. Yeon Cheol is already asleep.

fail.log: You lose patience, and win, beautifully. The crowd roars. Yeon Cheol goes in without a word and shuts the door, and you stand on the terrace with your fine victory and try to work out what to do with it. Next year.

choices.text: Bow, lay your sword down, and let him have the day

effects.log: He takes the day, and he takes your name along with it, and goes down the mountain a great man. You sweep the terrace after. Yeon Cheol comes and sweeps beside you, which he has never done.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Tutor Hwang Sun sets you the first examination: not an essay, but a county. You are to read three years of Magistrate Bang's tax books at Hanam and say what is wrong. There is a very great deal of paper, and all of it adds up. It adds up so very well, in fact, that on the fourth night you start to wonder who has been so careful, and why.

choices.text: Follow the neat figures down to where they stop being neat

ok.log: A grain store that has never once been short, in a county that has flooded twice. You lay it out in two pages. Hwang Sun reads them standing up. "Now you know what the job is," says the tutor, and passes you.

fail.log: You write ninety careful pages about a mistake in the salt tax. It is a real mistake, and it comes to nineteen coins. "You have found what you were allowed to find," says the tutor. Next year.

choices.text: Go down to Hanam and ask the farmers

effects.log: It costs you a season, and your shoes, and most of your dignity. Nobody has asked them before. You bring back a list in nine hands, and Hwang Sun passes you, and sighs at your shoes.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: Now you must take your two pages to Magistrate Bang himself. He is charming. He gives you very good tea. He explains, with real sadness, what would become of Hanam if the store were emptied and audited now, before the winter. He is not wrong. He also mentions, as if it had only just occurred to him, a post in the capital.

choices.text: Keep him talking until he offers you the real figures

ok.log: You have never been so polite in your life. By the third pot he has shown you the second set of books, in order to explain why they are necessary. You thank him. You sign nothing, and you report all of it.

fail.log: He out-teas you. You walk out with a promise, a basket of pears, and nothing on paper. It takes you three days to notice. Next year, says Hwang Sun, eating a pear.

choices.text: Refuse the tea, and read the charge aloud in his own hall

effects.log: It is the rudest thing that has been done in Hanam in a generation. Nobody will invite you anywhere for years. But it is on the record now, and a record is what you were sent for.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The flood comes anyway, in the eighth month. Bang has fled, the store is half empty, and for no reason anyone will later be able to explain, the county seal has ended up in your hand. Four thousand people stand on the dike road looking at you. You are not a magistrate. There is no regulation for this. Tutor Hwang Sun, up to the knees in water, has just asked you what the regulation is.

choices.text: Write the regulation, now, on the dike road, and sign it

ok.log: You write eleven lines and sign them. Then you see to it they are obeyed. Nobody starves that winter, and in the spring you turn yourself in to the prefect for using a seal not yours. He reads it, and burns it, and bows.

fail.log: You send to the prefect for orders, as you should. They arrive in nine days, in very good order, and it is nine days too late for a village called Lower Sang. Nobody blames you, by the book. Next year.

choices.text: Empty your own purse into the grain boats, and answer for it later

effects.log: There is no regulation for that either. Every coin you own goes down the river, and comes back as rice. Hwang Sun enters it in the book under a heading of the tutor's own invention.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Old Banner Cheon sends you to the ferry at Ma's Landing to deliver a letter and be back in a week. You get there to find the widow who runs the ferry being leaned on by a salt merchant's men, very quietly and legally. You were told a week. The letter is sealed, and looks urgent. Widow Ma has not asked you for a thing, and she is not going to.

choices.text: Go to the merchant with her ledgers, and talk it through

ok.log: It takes three weeks. He backs off, though he smiles as he does it. You go home late, with the letter, and hand it to Cheon. He opens it. It is blank. "Three weeks," he says. "That is about right."

fail.log: You talk well, and the merchant talks better, and you leave having made it worse. You stay on anyway, to work the ferry until something gives. That takes a season. The letter was blank. Next year.

choices.text: Sit on her landing with your sword across your knees until they tire of it

effects.log: They tire of it in about a month. It is a dull, wet, hungry month, and you are seen doing it by everybody on the river, and that was the idea. The letter was blank. Cheon nods.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: Captain Ro, who once stood beside you, has been accused of selling a pass to the Greenwood. Everyone knows it. The evidence is good and the hall is sharpening its voice. Ro asks only one thing of you: to stand next to him at the hearing, where everyone can see, and say nothing. You do not know if he did it. He will not tell you, and he says that is rather the point.

choices.text: Stand beside him, and take what comes of it

ok.log: You stand. People you have known for years look through you. At the end of it, the true seller is found by someone else, for reasons unrelated, and Ro buys you tea and does not thank you. You would have stood there either way, and you both know it.

fail.log: You stand, but your eyes go to the door when the charge is read, and Ro sees it. He is cleared in the end. He is very polite to you afterwards, and he always will be. Next year.

choices.text: Stand beside him, and say aloud you would do it again if he were guilty

effects.log: That is not what he asked for. It is a good deal worse for your name. The hall will not soon forget it, and neither, you notice, will Ro, who now keeps a chair for you by his fire.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last step is not arranged by anyone. A band of raiders has come over the Last Pass with a hundred and fifty riders, and the village below has an hour. Old Banner Cheon, who can hardly walk now, has got himself up onto the pass with the flag and two old friends, and has sat down on a rock in the middle of the road. He sent nobody word. Somebody told you anyway.

choices.text: Go up, and stand next to him

ok.log: You hold for the hour, then for most of another. Cheon does not get up from the rock. When it is over there are a good many people on the road, and one of the two old friends is singing very badly. The flag has a new hole, and he has you darn it.

fail.log: You get there too late for the first charge, and two of them have fallen. Cheon, wounded, is still sitting on his rock. "You came," he says. He does not say it the way you would like. Next year, if there is a next year.

choices.text: Go up, and carry the flag down the far side, to draw them off

effects.log: They chase it for eleven miles. You are not in good shape by the end, and neither is the flag. Cheon receives what is left of it and spends a long while looking at it, then hands you the needle.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Toll-Mother Gang tells you there is no trial, go and take something. So you are on the Heron Road when Big Deok, the largest person you have ever seen, comes down it the other way, with four mules. He runs that road. Everybody on it pays him, and he is very cheerful about it. He has just asked you, in a friendly way, what you think you are looking at.

choices.text: Take the mules from him, then give him a job

ok.log: It goes on until sunset. In the end he is lying on his back, laughing, with a split lip. "Nobody has done that since my mother," he says. He works for you now, and he tells everyone, and that is your first step.

fail.log: He picks you up and sets you in a tree, without malice. You get down in the morning. Nobody on the Heron Road has ever been this polite to you, and you can feel them not laughing for miles. Next year.

choices.text: Take a beating, come back the next morning, and take another

effects.log: On the fifth morning he says, "Oh, for the love of heaven," and gives you one of the mules. You did not win. You passed anyway, and everyone in the stronghold knows the difference, and likes you for it.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: Now take something you cannot take by hitting it. Scar Pyo holds the river crossing with sixty men, and he has held it for twenty years, and he has not slept two nights in one place in all that time. You have nine men. Gang gives you a season, chewing. "The strong eat," she says. "Nobody said with what teeth."

choices.text: Buy his cooks, and wait

ok.log: You spend a season buying nothing but soup. By the end his men eat your food, tell your cooks their troubles, and think of the crossing as a job. Pyo sees it just too late, and laughs till it hurts, and leaves by the back way with his life.

fail.log: You buy the wrong cook. Pyo sends the soup back to you, with the cook, and a very civil note. It is the most frightening thing you have ever been sent. Next year.

choices.text: Walk in alone and call him out in front of the sixty

effects.log: It should not work. It very nearly does not. But sixty men have been waiting twenty years to see if the old man still could, and he finds, in the end, that he cannot. You carry the scar for good.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: Gang is dying, and she knows it, and it has made her cheerful. She has you and three others up to the roof, and hands out the knife to nobody. "The roads are taxed by whoever can," she says. "So. Can you?" The three others have their hands near their sleeves. All of you know that there is more than one way of being the last one left on a roof.

choices.text: Beat all three, and send none of them off the roof

ok.log: It is a very long morning, and nobody dies. When it is over they are all sitting against the wall with you, breathing, and you find that you have just acquired three lieutenants. Gang has been asleep through the second half of it. Or she wants you to think so.

fail.log: You are the first one thrown down the stairs. It is a low roof, and a long time before anyone stops laughing. Next year, says Gang, if she lives. She does, purely to see it.

choices.text: Sit down next to Gang, and tell them to come and take it

effects.log: It is the most insulting thing they have ever seen. One tries. After that, nobody does. Gang pats your knee, with her terrible hand, and you have your first ever feeling of what she has been so tired of all these years.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Aunt Dok gives you a bowl of something and a sick dog and tells you to find out what it is. The dog is very patient. It looks at you with complete trust. There are forty jars on the shelf, and you know what thirty-one of them do. The needle-girl Suri, who is eleven and has done this before, is watching you with her chin on her hands.

choices.text: Work out which jar, slowly, from the dog

ok.log: It takes three days and no sleep. The dog gets up on the third evening and eats your dinner. Aunt Dok tells you which of your guesses would have killed it, in order, and how many there were. You pass.

fail.log: You guess wrong, and fortunately so does the bowl, which was mostly chalk. The dog is fine, and now it does not trust you. Suri shows you the right jar, with some pity. Next year.

choices.text: Take the same bowl yourself, so you can feel what it does

effects.log: You spend four days on the floor, and you do find out. So does the dog, who gets the right jar at last, and spends the rest of the week lying on your feet.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A guest has come to Aunt Dok's fire: Apothecary Ham, who poisoned her brother, thirty years ago, and who has come himself now, in the rain, because he is dying and nobody else can cure it. She has fed him. She has given you the needle and gone to bed. "Never turn on a guest," she says over her shoulder. "I said nothing about being good at it."

choices.text: Cure him, as well as it can be done

ok.log: It is the finest work you have ever done, on the worst man you have ever met. He gets up in a week, weeps, and goes away. Aunt Dok finds the jars all clean in the morning. She does not say anything, but she leaves you her second-best needle.

fail.log: Your hands are not as sure as you thought. He lives, but he will limp and stammer, and you honestly cannot say whether you meant it. Neither can she. She takes the needle back. Next year.

choices.text: Cure him, and pay for every herb yourself

effects.log: She will not let a coin of the house be spent on him, and now you know why you were asked. Your purse goes into him, leaf by leaf. He never finds out.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: A fever has reached the valley town of Ogri. It is not a natural one. The well has been fouled, and you know whose work it is, because you know the mix: it came from your own house, sold years ago to someone who said it was for rats. The town has shut its gates, with the sick inside, and it is asking who will go in. Suri has already packed.

choices.text: Go in with her, and find the cure inside the walls

ok.log: Forty days. You make the cure from what they have, and when the gates open Suri walks out in front of you, taller than you remember. Nobody in Ogri ever learns where it came from, and you tell Aunt Dok so to her face.

fail.log: You find the cure, but late. The town lives, and more of it would have, and Suri is very quiet on the way home. Aunt Dok looks at your hands, and then away. Next year.

choices.text: Go in, and tell them at the gate whose poison it is

effects.log: They very nearly stone you. Then they let you work, because who else is there, and they stand over you while you do it. It is the longest forty days of your life, and at the end someone brings you a bowl of soup.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Lamp Elder Mok tells you that the first step is simple: take the chair of the senior above you on the stairs. Everyone is watching to see how. The senior is a quiet person named Jeon, who has never harmed you, and who taught you where the good lamp oil is kept. Jeon, it seems, has already heard. Jeon has come to your room to say that it is all right, and there are no hard feelings.

choices.text: Beat Jeon fairly on the stairs, with the whole hall watching

ok.log: It is quick. Jeon gets up, bows and moves one chair down, and you sit in the one that is still warm. Nobody says well done. That night, without being asked, someone brings you the good oil.

fail.log: Jeon is better than Jeon ever let on. You wake at the bottom of the stairs. Your chair has not moved. Jeon brings you tea and is just as kind as before, and that is what frightens you. Next year.

choices.text: Let the hall know a thing about Jeon that you were told in confidence

effects.log: It works by morning. Jeon moves one chair down, and does not come to your room again. Mok looks at you for some time over the lamp. You are passed, and something else has also happened, and you know it.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: In the Hall of Lamps every disciple tends one flame, and yours has burned for eight years. The second step: you must put out someone else's. Mok gives you the list of those whose lamps could be spared, and it is told to you very plainly what a lamp stands for here. Nobody expects you to enjoy it. Several people on that list are expecting you. One has left you a note.

choices.text: Find a name on that list who has earned it

ok.log: You spend a season finding out. Most of them have. You choose, and what happens then is told in the hall in nine words, and you tend your own flame a little more carefully after that.

fail.log: You choose in a hurry, and you choose wrong: the name was on the list as a test. The whole hall knows by morning. Your own lamp has been moved to the draughty end of the hall. Next year.

choices.text: Put out your own, and start again from a new wick

effects.log: Nobody has done that in living memory. It costs you eight years' worth of something the hall does not put a name to, and it costs you sleep. Mok sits down beside you that night, and does not mention it.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last step is an offer. The Cult has a prisoner, an orthodox elder who taught half the men who hunt you, and who is very old. You are to go in, alone, and come out having got from them the name of the one who sold out the Cult's northern halls. How is your own affair. It will not be asked about. You will not be thanked. The elder has seen many like you, and looks glad of the company.

choices.text: Beat the elder at their own game, over many nights, in words

ok.log: Nobody ever hears what you said to each other. You come out on the twentieth day with the name, and the elder, as far as anyone can tell, is sleeping well. Lamp Elder Mok looks at you, for the first time, as if you might be dangerous.

fail.log: On the twentieth night you notice that you have told them rather more than they have told you. You stop going. There is an entry in the book, and it is not a kind one. Next year.

choices.text: Pay the price they ask for it: something of yours, told to nobody

effects.log: They name a thing. You give it up. It will not be set down here, and you will not be telling it either. You come out with the name, and the hall makes room for you, and you find you do not much like the warmth.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Ledger Sister Ran turns to your page. It shows a debt, entered on the day you came. "The first payment," she says, and sends you to collect from Old Debtor Bae, who owes the Ancestor forty years of something and keeps a duck. He cannot pay. He knows it. He has made you some soup. There is a story, told downstairs, about what becomes of a collector who comes back with nothing.

choices.text: Work out what Bae really has that the book will take

ok.log: He has forty years of knowing where everything in this valley is buried. You write it down, for three days, and he seems relieved. Ran reads it, and rules off his page in red. The duck looks at you as if you owed it.

fail.log: You come back with the duck. It is entered, gravely, at the value of one duck. Sister Ran does not laugh, and that is the problem. Next year.

choices.text: Pay Bae's debt out of your own breath, and take it onto your page

effects.log: It goes down in red. You feel it, in the mornings, as you might feel a stair you have missed. Ran rules off his page, and looks at yours a little longer than is comfortable.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: The second payment is told to you in the dark, in the old way, by someone you never see: name one you are fond of, and give up being fond of them. Nothing will be done to them. Nothing will be done at all. It will simply be noted, and held, and you will know. Sister Ran waits on the far side of the door with the book, as if it were an ordinary sort of evening.

choices.text: Find what the rule really takes, and give only that

ok.log: It takes you a month to find the wording. You can go on helping them. You can go on being kind. You give up being thanked. It is entered, and Ran reads it, and raises one eyebrow, the first you have ever seen move.

fail.log: You try to find a way round, and there is none you can find. You say no name. The door stays shut, and the page stays open. Next year.

choices.text: Give the name, and hold to it

effects.log: You give it, and nothing happens, and it goes on happening. They write to you at the new year. You read it, and you put it in a box. Nobody asks to see the box.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The third payment is a duel with your own debt. In the deep hall the Blood Ancestor's followers have a practice nobody outside has ever been told about, and it will not be told here. You go down the stairs alone. What stands at the bottom knows every entry on your page, and it wears your hands. Ran has tied the red cord to your wrist, and she has told you not to let it go slack.

choices.text: Fight it for your page, line by line

ok.log: It takes a night and a day. You come up the stairs with the cord still taut. Your page has been ruled off, in a hand you do not recognise, and a new page has been started in the same hand. Sister Ran bows to you. You had no idea she knew how.

fail.log: The cord goes slack. They pull you up by it, some time later. Nobody says anything, and your page is just as it was, plus one line. Next year.

choices.text: Agree with it: every line is true, and you will pay

effects.log: It is not what anyone expects of you down there. It stands a while, then it steps aside. The price of the way you chose goes on your page in red, and it will be a long time before you come to the end of it.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: A founder has no examiner, so the hall makes one. Your own disciples have gathered in the yard, and Big Deok, once a porter and now your oldest student, steps forward red in the face. "They say you could not beat us all at once any more," he says. "I told them I would ask." The creed on the wall says what it says.

choices.text: Take them all at once

ok.log: It lasts until the lamps are lit. Nobody can stand up afterwards, you included, and the yard has never been so happy. The creed holds.

fail.log: They get you down on the ninth rush. There is a dreadful silence, then Deok helps you up, and that is worse. Next year.

choices.text: Take them one at a time until the last is done, however long

effects.log: It takes three days. Nobody goes home. By the end they are bringing you water between bouts.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A greater house has sent an envoy to say your creed is a boast. Strength above all? Then come and be measured, on their ground, by their rules. It is plainly a trap. The whole of your hall has heard. Big Deok has started to crack his knuckles.

choices.text: Go, and win by their own rules

ok.log: You read their rules for a week before you go, and it turns out they forgot to forbid a number of things. They will not make that mistake twice.

fail.log: Their rules hold. You come home with a loss, entered in somebody else's book. Next year.

choices.text: Go, and take a loss on your feet in front of them all

effects.log: They beat you, and it takes them all day. You walk out of their gate unaided. Word of that travels further than any win would have.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The third step is one you always knew about. The best student you ever taught has come back from the road, stronger than when they left, and has asked very politely for the seat. It is the creed. It is written on your own wall. The hall has gone quiet and has found reasons to be in the yard.

choices.text: Meet them, and win

ok.log: It is the best fight of your life. You win it by about a hand's breadth. You offer them the second chair, and you are honest with them about how close it was.

fail.log: You lose the first exchange badly, and they stop, and bow, and say they will come back when you are ready. It is unbearable. Next year.

choices.text: Meet them, knowing you may lose, and say so to the hall first

effects.log: You say it aloud, and then you fight, and it goes on until neither of you can. The hall calls it a draw, out of love. The creed stays on the wall.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: You founded a house on the Dao alone, and it now has a kitchen budget. An old friend, Cloud-Keeper Mu, visits and looks round, kindly. "So many roofs," Mu says. "How long since you sat under no roof at all?" You open your mouth to answer. It has been eleven years.

choices.text: Go out with Mu, tonight, and leave the keys

ok.log: Nothing happens for a month, and it is wonderful. The hall has survived too, somewhat to your annoyance. You pass.

fail.log: You last four days, and then you are thinking about the kitchen budget. Mu says nothing at all, in a marked manner. Next year.

choices.text: Give away a third of everything the hall owns

effects.log: It hurts more than you expected, and the disciples grumble for a season. Then the place is quieter, and you can hear the rain.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A prefect comes in full robes to offer your hall a charter, a tax exemption, and his son as a pupil. All he wants is a small plaque saying so. The disciples are very excited. Your roof leaks. Mu, who has not left, is eating a pear in the corner and enjoying this.

choices.text: Decline so gracefully he thanks you

ok.log: He goes home thinking it was his own idea. The roof goes on leaking. The son turns up a year later on foot, with no robes, and you take him.

fail.log: You decline, and he hears an insult in it. It will be some years before the road to your gate is mended. Next year.

choices.text: Refuse flat, and let the disciples hate you for it

effects.log: Some leave. Those who stay stop asking about the roof. Mu passes you the other half of the pear.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: Your hall is doing well, and that is the third step. They have started to call you a great master. Pilgrims come. There is talk of a statue. Mu has died, quietly, and left you a note with one line in it: "Who is holding all this up?"

choices.text: Find out, by walking away for a year, and see

ok.log: It stands. It stands rather better, in fact. You come back and sweep the yard, and when somebody asks for the great master you tell them truthfully you have not seen one.

fail.log: You stay to make sure of things first, and the first thing leads to a second. There is a statue by autumn. Next year.

choices.text: Knock the statue down yourself, in front of the pilgrims

effects.log: It takes a good many blows. They go home confused, then they come back quieter. The note goes into the fire, and you feel Mu laughing.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Headwoman Ahn has come up with a list of everything your creed has promised, and it is longer than you remember. The bridges, the well, the tax. This is your first step, she says, and she will be judging it herself. She has brought lunch, so as to judge it in comfort.

choices.text: Talk the prefect's clerk out of the tax

ok.log: Nine visits and a good deal of patience, and the clerk discovers an old exemption. Ahn crosses off one line, and looks at the next.

fail.log: The clerk sees you coming. The village pays the tax and a fine for asking. Ahn crosses off nothing, and she stays for dinner. Next year.

choices.text: Mend the two bridges with your own hands

effects.log: Your disciples watch their founder carry stones for a month. A few come and help, and then they all do. Ahn says the left one is crooked.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A hungry winter, and the granary at your hall holds enough for your own for a year, or for the valley for two months. Your steward lays out the sums, white-faced. The cook, Bok-nam, has already started to boil water. "How many, then?" Bok-nam asks. "I need a number."

choices.text: Plan it out so nobody starves and the hall holds

ok.log: You split it, trade your silver for grain, and send the strong to hunt. It is thin soup in every bowl in the valley, and every bowl has some. You lose nobody.

fail.log: The sums come out wrong in the seventh week. There are graves, not many, and you know the names. Next year.

choices.text: Open the doors, and let the hall go hungry too

effects.log: All of you are thinner by spring, you most of all. Three disciples leave. Those who stay have a look about them you would not trade.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: An army is coming through the valley, and it is nobody's enemy. It is merely hungry. Its general has sent a very reasonable letter to you, one great master to another, proposing that you stand aside and your hall will not be touched. Ahn, very old now, has walked up the hill to see what you will write back. She has not brought lunch.

choices.text: Stand in the road, and make the general find another way

ok.log: You do not fight the army. You fight the first three who are sent to move you, and then the general, who is no fool, finds another way. The valley never learns how close it was. Ahn does.

fail.log: You hold the road a day and a half. They go round by the farms. It could have been worse, and you will think about how it could have been better for the rest of your life. Next year.

choices.text: Pay the army to go round, with all you have

effects.log: The treasury of your hall goes into the general's wagons, down to the last string of coins. You go back to eating from the same pot as everyone else. Ahn says that it suits you.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Comptroller Sim has found an error in your hall's books. It is not in your favour, and nobody but Sim would ever have caught it. The money is owed to a family of river traders who think they were paid in full, thirty years ago, under the founder before the founder. "It is your move," says Sim, and sits very still.

choices.text: Find them, and settle it so it pays you both

ok.log: You pay every coin, with interest, and you also buy out their barge rights while you are there. They weep with gratitude. Sim adjusts one figure and permits themself a small nod.

fail.log: You reckon it a little short. They find out years later, as they would. Sim enters that too. Next year.

choices.text: Pay it in full, at the worst possible time

effects.log: It empties the spring accounts. Your disciples eat a great deal of barley. It is entered, in very good ink, and you find you sleep better.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: Moneychanger Noh holds your hall's paper, and has done for years. Noh proposes a new arrangement over dinner, very friendly: forgive the old debts of a certain county, and in return the county's magistrate will make you rich. It is entirely legal. Everything is paid for, Noh points out, smiling, with your own creed.

choices.text: Read the small print aloud at the table, and renegotiate

ok.log: You find it on page nine. By dessert the magistrate is paying you, and Noh is laughing with real delight, and has already started to plan revenge.

fail.log: Noh has read your creed far more carefully than you have. You sign, and it takes you two years to find out what. Next year.

choices.text: Refuse, and pay off the whole of Noh's paper at once

effects.log: It costs you a great deal more than it should. But nobody in this province now holds a single sheet with your name on it.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last account. A plague year, and every house in the province owes you now, down to the temple. You could own it all by spring. Clerk Yu brings you the total in a shaking hand. "It is all legal," Yu says, and looks as if they would be sick. "Every debt is written down. That is what we swore."

choices.text: Reprice every debt so they can all pay, and you still profit

ok.log: It takes the whole winter and it is the finest bookkeeping of your life. Everyone pays, slowly, for twenty years. The province thinks of you as a kind of weather, and it brings an umbrella.

fail.log: You miss one village in the arithmetic. By spring it is yours and empty. You keep the entry where you can see it. Next year.

choices.text: Write it all down, then burn the book in the market

effects.log: It was written down. You said nothing about keeping it. Sim weeps, the only time anyone has seen it. You are poorer than you have been in decades, and no one in the province will ever again refuse you anything.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: List-Keeper Gyo opens the book to the oldest name on it. The person is alive, seventy, and keeps bees. The wrong was real. "You swore that none is forgiven for nothing," says Gyo. "That is the first step: what is it to cost them, and why that?" A jar of honey has come from them every autumn. You had not noticed that until now.

choices.text: Go and ask what they think they owe

ok.log: A long afternoon. It turns out that they know exactly. They name a sum and a thing to say aloud, and they pay it, and you strike the name. Your hand shakes, and you are annoyed about that.

fail.log: You go to ask, and you end up shouting. A bee stings you. The name stays where it is, and you go home feeling that it was the wrong person shouting. Next year.

choices.text: Take the honey, and leave the name on, and tell them why

effects.log: It is very quiet by the hives. They nod. The jars go on coming. You find that a name can be carried without being a weight.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A boy named Nam has walked to your gate with a list of his own, and your hall's name is on it. Some years ago your people did a thing in your name. You never asked. It is all true. He is fourteen, and he is shaking, and he asks you to teach him so that he can do this properly.

choices.text: Teach him, and tell him where the wrong is written in your book

ok.log: You enter it yourself, in your own hand, on your own page. He stays nine years. It is not at all clear how this ends, but it is at least properly recorded.

fail.log: You send him away with money. He does not take it. You will be seeing him again, and this time he will have learned somewhere else. Next year.

choices.text: Pay his family what the book says it was worth

effects.log: It is a very large figure, and you make your own elders watch you count it out. Nam stands by the gate and does not thank you, as you taught everyone not to.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last name on the first page: the one who began all of it. Gyo has found them at last, and they are very great now, and they do not remember you at all. You could go up to their hall tomorrow and end it. Your disciples are ready. Nam is ready. They are all looking at you, and you realise the whole of your house is built on this morning.

choices.text: Go up alone, in the open, and make them remember

ok.log: They do, by the end. You do not take their life, and they will never again sleep well. You strike the name, with a hand that does not shake, and you look up and do not know what to do with your afternoon.

fail.log: They are stronger than the story of them. You are carried home, and the name stays. Your disciples tell it as a beginning. Next year.

choices.text: Strike the name without going, and tell the hall why

effects.log: It costs you half of your disciples. They say you have lost your nerve. You have lost something, and you are not sure yet that it was nerve. Gyo closes the book, and leaves it closed.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: Nobody examines a throne, so old Tutor Hwang Sun, who taught you your letters and fears nothing, has simply brought the petitions up from the outer gate: the ones your ministers decided you need not see. There are two hundred. The tutor sets them on the footstool, and sits down to watch you read.

choices.text: Read them all, and find what they have in common

ok.log: It takes eleven nights, and they have one name in common. You do not raise your voice at the morning audience. By noon there is a vacancy, and the tutor nods as if you had got a sum right.

fail.log: You read them, and you are moved, and you pardon a good many people who should not have been. The tutor reads your decrees and sighs. Next year.

choices.text: Go out to the gate and hear them in person

effects.log: Your guards are appalled. So are your ministers. It rains. You sit under an umbrella until the line is finished, and people tell it to their grandchildren.

choices.text: Bow, and ask for another year

effects.log: Nobody reproaches you. That step will still be there, and so will they.

events.text: A minister you trust has done something unforgivable for your own good, and it has worked: the border is quiet. Everyone knows it. Everyone is waiting to see whether the rule you swore to applies to those who serve you well. He has come to the hall in plain robes, without being asked, and knelt.

choices.text: Judge him by the law, in the open, and keep him if the law allows

ok.log: It takes a month of hearings. He loses his post and his name, and he keeps his life, and he thanks you. You will never have so good a minister again. The whole court now reads the law carefully.

fail.log: You look for a way to spare him, and everybody can see you looking. It is the worst of both, and the court notes it. Next year.

choices.text: Take the fault on yourself, in a public decree

effects.log: A ruler's edict of self-reproach is a rare thing. It costs you more than a lost province. He goes home in tears, and the provinces read it aloud.

choices.text: Say you are not ready

effects.log: It is noted without comment. In this house, that is a kind of courtesy.

events.text: The last step comes from no one. You have reigned long enough to know where it all goes. Your heir is not ready, your ministers are not honest, and everyone in the palace would prefer you to live forever. Tutor Hwang Sun, very old, has asked for one last audience, and asks one question: "Who would you hand it to tonight, and have you told them why?"

choices.text: Sit down with your heir and hold nothing back

ok.log: Three nights, with no attendants. It is the hardest thing you have ever said to anyone. You come out older, and so do they. The tutor dies that winter, and you carry the bier yourself, as the rites require and nobody expected.

fail.log: You begin, and find you cannot say the worst of it. You talk about the harvest instead. The tutor closes their eyes. Next year, if there is one.

choices.text: Write all of it down, seal it, and put it in the hall for whoever comes

effects.log: It is a very long document. You sign it. You find that, having signed it, you rule rather better, as one who has already been read.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home, and you think about it, and it does you more good than you would have guessed.

events.text: The man who killed a friend of yours is kneeling in the road with his sword broken. He is laughing, a little. He knows about your vow, and he has told the crowd about it. "So I can do this as often as I like, then," he says.

choices.text: Bind his hands, and hand him to the magistrate

effects.log: It is very dull. The magistrate is slow. You go home, and you hit nothing, and it takes you some hours to unclench your hand.

choices.text: Finish it

effects.log: It takes no time at all. Nobody in the road will meet your eye, and you know what that was you just set down.

events.text: A rich widow leaves you a house with a pear orchard, in gratitude. It is lovely. You are told that it comes with no duties at all. You catch yourself working out where you would put the bench.

choices.text: Give it to the alms road, and keep one pear

effects.log: It is a very good pear. You think about the bench for roughly another nine years.

choices.text: Keep the house

effects.log: It is a wonderful house, and you sit on the bench. You swore to keep nothing you do not need, and you are finding reasons why you need it.

events.text: The governor is dead and the province is coming apart. A deputation has climbed your mountain to beg you to take the seat, just for a year or two. They are right, is the trouble: you would be good at it. There are eleven of them and they have brought the seal.

choices.text: Send them to someone better, and go back to your sweeping

effects.log: You give them three names and a good lunch. The province muddles through. You will wonder about it on bad nights.

choices.text: Take the seal

effects.log: It is heavier than it looks. You are very good at it. You swore not to, and you know exactly what this is.

events.text: A rival master has called you a coward in front of the whole Wulin Gathering, and your own students are burning. You could end this with one sword-stroke. Yielding has been easy, all these years, when nobody was watching.

choices.text: Bow, and let it pass

effects.log: You bow. The silence goes on a while. Somewhere around the third year after that, people begin to wonder who won.

choices.text: Meet force with force, in front of everyone

effects.log: It is magnificent. Everyone says so. You have not moved like that in decades, and you feel the Soft Way close behind you like a door.

events.text: Your deputy has made a small error in an old report. It would be simple to correct the date and say nothing. It would save a good man his post. Nobody could ever find out, and you have the brush in your hand.

choices.text: Report it as it stands, and go to bat for him

effects.log: You sign it, and go and speak for him, at some cost to yourself. He loses a year's pay. He keeps the post, and he will not meet your eye for a long time.

choices.text: Change the date

effects.log: One stroke. It does not even look different. You wrote something you would not sign, and your name is on it.

events.text: A very old friend is running from the law, for a crime that was not much of a crime. They are at your back door in the rain. "Just tonight," they say. There is a warrant on your desk with their name on it, waiting for your seal.

choices.text: Seal it, and give them what is in your purse

effects.log: They look at you for a long moment, then take the purse, and go. They are caught at the river. You visit them every month.

choices.text: Hide them

effects.log: A dry bed and a hot meal, and they are gone by morning, safe, and you have put your name on the wrong side of the law.

events.text: You are one day from everything you have worked for. The summons is in your hand, and the road is long. And a boy has just run up to say that your old friend Ro is cornered at Stone Ford with four men, and could use you. It is the wrong way entirely. Ro will understand. Ro would be the first to say so.

choices.text: Turn the horse round

effects.log: You arrive in time. Ro is furious with you for coming, and you have lost the summons, and will never get another one. You drink a great deal that night.

choices.text: Ride on

effects.log: You make your appointment. It goes very well. Ro lives, as it happens, and sends you a note of congratulations, and you burn it.

events.text: The Greenwood has offered you peace for your valley, on one condition: an old woman who gave them trouble, whom they would like handed over. She is no kin of yours. Your people are looking at you, and they have children, and they are not wicked people at all.

choices.text: Say no, and get ready

effects.log: It costs you the east fields and a good many nights. She dies in her own bed, very cross about the noise. Your people forgive you, mostly.

choices.text: Hand her over

effects.log: The valley is safe. It is very safe. People bow to you in the road, and they look a little past you when they do it.

events.text: A prince has heard of you, and sends a golden collar, more or less: a retainer's post, at a price that would feed your people for ten years. You could beat him with one hand and you both know it. All he asks is that you come when you are called.

choices.text: Send back the gold, with one of his own teeth

effects.log: You keep to the road, and your people go on eating what they take. The prince is much politer now. So is everybody.

choices.text: Put it on

effects.log: The food is excellent, and you come when you are called. You took a leash from someone weaker, and everybody on the road knows it by spring.

events.text: You lost, this morning. A girl of nineteen on the Heron Road put you on your back in front of your own men. You are bigger, you are richer, and you have sixty people who would quietly see to it tonight if you only nodded. She is asleep in the inn with her boots off.

choices.text: Go down to the inn in the morning and offer her your chair

effects.log: She says no, laughing, and takes your best horse instead. You keep your chair only because she does not want it. That is the law, and you have just kept it.

choices.text: Nod

effects.log: It is seen to. Nobody mentions it. The strong eat, you swore, and you have just let everyone find out what you are when you are not.

events.text: The man at your fire is the one who betrayed your house to the Tang. He does not know that you know. He has eaten your salt. He is telling a very funny story, and there are three jars within reach of your left hand, and it would look entirely like his heart.

choices.text: Fill his cup with honest wine, and see him to the gate

effects.log: He leaves in the morning, cheerful and very alive. You wash the cup twice. You will meet him on the road some day, and it will not be at your fire.

choices.text: Reach for the third jar

effects.log: It looks entirely like his heart. You have made a very neat job of it. You swore on this very fire, and it is burning just the same.

events.text: A lord is paying a king's ransom for a poison with no cure. It is a pure problem, the most interesting one you have seen in years, and you are fairly sure that you could do it. He does not mind what you do afterwards. He only wants there to be no second jar.

choices.text: Make the cure first, and send the lord both, with your bill

effects.log: He is enraged. He pays, though. The cure goes to every physician in the province, and you have made a dangerous friend of nobody.

choices.text: Make it, and make no cure

effects.log: It is beautiful work. You are extremely well paid. Every poison has its cure, you swore, and you have just made a thing in the world with none.

events.text: A village has taken you in, badly hurt, not knowing what you are. An old woman has fed you for a month from very little. Your wounds are healed now, and the Cult's rule is clear about witnesses. You find you have learned the names of her grandchildren.

choices.text: Do what the rule asks of you: burn the place down around your own softness, and go

effects.log: You take what you came with and leave them a warning in red. They run for the hills, and they live, and they hate you. Nobody in the hall can call that soft. You know exactly what it was.

choices.text: Stay another month and mend her roof

effects.log: It is a good roof. The whole valley is talking about it. You have gone soft, and you are happy, and the Red Clerk will know by the new moon.

events.text: A junior has failed you, in front of the hall, and now kneels. Everyone is waiting. It is a small thing that the rule asks of you here, told in one word. The junior is very young, and has a stammer that you know they have worked hard on.

choices.text: Say the word, with the whole hall watching

effects.log: It is told in the hall that night, in nine words. Nobody fails you again. It is not as if you have to be fond of the silence.

choices.text: Have them sent to the kitchens, and say no more

effects.log: The hall stares. You know what they have just seen. The stammering junior will be loyal to you for life, and it will do neither of you any good.

events.text: The day of payment has come round and your page shows you short. Old Debtor Bae, of all people, has come to tell you how you could quietly move a figure, as he did for eleven years. Ledger Sister Ran is ill, and nobody is reading the book this season.

choices.text: Pay what is written, however it hurts

effects.log: It hurts. The page is square. Bae shakes his head at you, and offers you his duck, in sympathy.

choices.text: Move the figure

effects.log: One stroke. Nobody will ever know, you tell yourself, and then you remember whose book it is.

events.text: A girl has been brought to the Cult for what she might be worth. It is your turn to see to her. She reminds you of nobody. That is what is so annoying, because you cannot even blame that. Nobody would ever look to see which way she went out of the back gate.

choices.text: See to her as the Ancestor asks, and do not look back

effects.log: It is told, and entered, and it will never be shown here. You sleep very well that night. That is the thing you will think about, some nights, in years to come.

choices.text: Open the back gate

effects.log: She runs without thanking you. You stand there with the key in your hand. You have gone soft, and it is written down somewhere, whatever anybody says.

events.text: A bad year, and the whole province is at your gate. Your treasurer has found a way to save the hall: close it, for one winter, to everyone but your own. Just this once. Your disciples have children too, and they are looking at you.

choices.text: Keep it open

effects.log: You are nearly ruined by spring. Several people leave. The gate is known from here to the sea, and the people who came through it remember.

choices.text: Close the gate

effects.log: Your own come through the winter fat. You can see the road from your window. You have stopped looking out of that window.

events.text: The prefect offers you the village of Lower Sang, free and clear, if you will sign off on moving its people to make way for the salt road. It would pay for your hall for a generation. They would be paid something. They would not be asked.

choices.text: Refuse, and go and tell them

effects.log: They do not thank you. They ask what you mean to do about it, which is the right question, and you are up all night with them.

choices.text: Sign

effects.log: It is a very good road, and the hall has a new roof, and you can no longer ride through there.

events.text: A great debtor of yours has died owing you more than your hall is worth. Nobody else has seen the note. Your clerk Yu hints that the entry could quietly stay in the book as paid to someone else, and the money could go elsewhere, and everybody would be better off.

choices.text: Enter it as it is, and pay the tax on it

effects.log: Clerk Yu looks unhappy. The tax is appalling. Your name, in six provinces, is still good for a thousand taels on a handshake.

choices.text: Lose the entry

effects.log: It goes very smoothly. Yu looks at you a little differently, and you notice that your books are harder to read now, even for you.

events.text: Your oldest friend owes you a sum that will finish them. They have asked you, without much hope, to forget it. They would never ask twice. You know their children. There is a lot to be said for mercy, and it has nothing to say about your oath.

choices.text: Hold them to it, and lend them the money to pay

effects.log: It takes them nineteen years. They do it. You do not dine together anymore, but they send a note when it is done, in a very steady hand.

choices.text: Tear up the note

effects.log: They weep. You do too, a bit. You are also now a person whose debts can be argued with, and by autumn everyone has heard.

events.text: One on the list has come to you, dying, and begs you to strike their name for nothing, because of the old days. There were old days. They have a very small voice now. No one would blame you. You would not even have to tell anybody.

choices.text: Name a price they can still pay, and take it

effects.log: It is a small thing: a true account, in their own words, to the family. They manage it in an hour. You strike the name, and you sit with them, and nothing is owed.

choices.text: Strike it, for nothing

effects.log: They die very peacefully. So do a good many of the other names, in the sense that the whole list no longer quite means what it said.

events.text: You have a new enemy, a great one, and the two of you could make a very profitable peace, if only you both set your lists aside. Their envoy is charming. It would cost you nothing but one old page that nobody else has read for years.

choices.text: Keep the page, and let the peace go

effects.log: The war is long and expensive. You could not say that it was worth it. But there is still one person in the murim who knows that nothing is forgotten.

choices.text: Burn the page

effects.log: It is an excellent peace. Your house flourishes. Some years later you find you cannot remember whose handwriting that was.

events.text: You go up to the sitting room with the bad window and take your anger with you, as requested. It has come along very willingly. There is somebody it wants to talk about. The hours go by. Your knees hurt, and it is still talking.

choices.text: Stay until it has run out of things to say

effects.log: Nine days. It repeats itself a good deal by the end. When you get up, the gate has the look of a door someone has left unlocked.

choices.text: Get up, this is not the year

effects.log: You get up. It comes down the stairs with you, quite cheerful, and the gate stays where it is.

events.text: Elder Beopjin hands you a broom and points at the long stairs. A thousand and eighty steps. You swept them as a novice, and they have never been clean, because of the trees. "Well?" the elder says.

choices.text: Sweep, and stop asking how many are left

effects.log: Leaves come down behind you all day. Somewhere in the second week you find that you like the sound. The gate can wait, and for that reason it does not.

choices.text: Say you will come back in the autumn, when the trees are bare

effects.log: The elder nods. The leaves go on. You have the feeling this has been said on these stairs before.

events.text: A season alone on the mountain with nothing to do. You have done this before and you are better at it than you were: you only bring one book. By the second week you have read it. By the third you have started talking to it.

choices.text: Throw the book in the stream, and sit

effects.log: It floats for some time. You watch it go. Nothing happens for the rest of the season, very thoroughly, and you come down with the gate standing open in you.

choices.text: Go back for another book

effects.log: It is a good book. You come down in a month, somewhat better read, and the gate has not been following the plot.

events.text: The goatherd Ji is a grown woman now, with goats of her own, and she lets you have the shed on the top pasture, where nobody will want you for anything. "What do you do up there?" she asks, every time. You have never yet found a good answer.

choices.text: Stay till you have stopped looking for one

effects.log: She comes up at the end of the season with a cheese. "Well?" she says. You cannot think what she means, and she nods, and goes back down.

choices.text: Tell her you are busy this year

effects.log: She shrugs. The shed will be there. So, it seems, will your answer.

events.text: Your office has a backlog, as it always has: nineteen petitions from people who have given up hope. The gate waits on this. It is, you will admit, a very strange way to run a heaven. You sharpen your brush.

choices.text: Do all nineteen, and do them properly

effects.log: You read them all. Four of the petitioners are dead by now, and you write to their children. When the last is signed, something settles in you, with a small, dry click, like a seal coming down.

choices.text: Do the easy ones, and leave the rest for next year

effects.log: Eleven are done. Eight are still waiting, and so is the gate, and it is keeping a neat record.

events.text: The inspector is coming, and for once you want him to find everything. You lay out your accounts, your rulings and your mistakes, in that order, and have the mistakes copied out twice. Your clerk thinks that you may have gone mad.

choices.text: Show him the mistakes first

effects.log: He reads them for a long while, then asks to see the rest, without much interest. He bows when he leaves. Your name is cleaner than it has ever been, and you are lighter by a good deal.

choices.text: Tidy them up a little first

effects.log: It would be easy, and you do it. The inspector is very pleased. The gate says nothing, in a way you have begun to recognise.

events.text: They are saying in the river towns that a man of the Tang has been cheating the widows of Stone Ford, and that nobody will speak up since he has a name. Your own name would do. You are told it is worth quite a lot now. You put on your good coat.

choices.text: Say it to his face, at noon, in the square

effects.log: He has friends and he brings them. It is a long afternoon, and everyone sees it. The widows get back about half. You are not as well thought of among the Tang now, and the gate is open.

choices.text: Send a letter instead

effects.log: It is a very fine letter. He has it framed. You keep your good coat clean.

events.text: A friend of yours from the old days has been named a traitor, and it may well be true. You have been asked to speak at the hearing in any way but the way you are going to. You find you already have your good coat on.

choices.text: Stand up where you can be seen, and speak for them

effects.log: It does not save them, much. It does not do you any good either. People who were not there will still be telling it in twenty years. You go home and the gate is open.

choices.text: Stay in the back, this time

effects.log: Nobody remarks on it. You get home early. The coat goes back on its peg, and you do not look at it.

events.text: There is a master at the Red Ford who has never been beaten, and you are told that he would very much enjoy it. You have not been afraid in a long time, and it occurs to you, walking there, that the road has a very pleasant view.

choices.text: Call him out

effects.log: It is the worst beating you have had in years. You get up four times. By the end he is holding your arm up for the crowd, whichever of you won. The gate does not care which.

choices.text: Admire the view, and go home

effects.log: It is a very pleasant view. You go home. Nobody on that road knows you went, and you do.

events.text: Six brothers have held the Salt Bridge for nine years and they have never once paid anyone for anything. They are expecting somebody, one day. They have made a very nice sign about it. You are standing in front of the sign.

choices.text: Read the sign aloud, and step on the bridge

effects.log: It takes until dark. They carry you to their fire afterwards and argue over which of them hit you hardest. You take the sign home. The gate seems to have been impressed.

choices.text: Pay the toll, for once

effects.log: The brothers count it, surprised. You walk across. The toll was very reasonable, and you feel it all the way home.

events.text: A carter's child at Ogri has the grey cough. You know the cure. It takes nine things and you own four of them, and no one on this road could pay for even one of the others. Aunt Dok has mentioned this child to you twice now, which from her is shouting.

choices.text: Buy what it takes, and go

effects.log: It takes all the coin you brought. The child gets up and at once bites you, and is told off. You come away with a bruise and a feeling that the gate has heard.

choices.text: Send a cheaper remedy, and hope

effects.log: It might do. You will not hear either way. Aunt Dok does not mention the child again.

events.text: Your needle-girl Suri has found a whole street in the river quarter with the same bad water, and she has made a list, and then costed it, and has left the page where you will find it. There is a very small sum at the bottom, in comparison to what you just paid for your new jars.

choices.text: Sell the new jars, and fix the street

effects.log: A hard month, and a very boring one, digging. The street stops coughing. Suri does not say anything, which is the first time she has not.

choices.text: Tell her next year, once the jars have paid for themselves

effects.log: She takes the page back, without comment. The jars are excellent.

events.text: At every gate the Red Clerk comes with the book and asks what you will give up this time. It is never what you would think. This time it is the memory of a song. You know the one. Someone used to hum it to you, when you were small. It would be taken out, and you would not miss it.

choices.text: Give it up

effects.log: He writes it down. You stand there for some time trying to think what you were so upset about. The gate is open. You hum something, walking back, and it is nothing.

choices.text: Not this one, not yet

effects.log: He closes the book without a word, and he will be back. The gate stays as it was, and so does the song.

events.text: The price this time is told in one line in the Hall of Lamps: someone who trusts you must stop trusting you, and it must be your doing. You are left to choose how. No one will be hurt, the Red Clerk adds. He is very particular about what the word means.

choices.text: Do it, to someone you would rather not

effects.log: It takes one short conversation. They look at you the way you are used to being looked at. It is told in nine words in the hall. The gate is open, and you do not look round.

choices.text: Tell the Clerk he can wait
