effects.log: He says that he can. He is very good at it. So far, nobody has outwaited him, and the gate agrees.

events.text: The payment for this gate is due. Sister Ran turns the book to you: a year of your life, in the old reckoning, or a year of somebody else's if you can find a willing lender. People have. It is all above board, she says, and she shows you the page.

choices.text: Pay it from your own account

effects.log: You feel it go, somewhere at the end of the line where you cannot see. She rules it off. It is told, and not shown. The gate is open.

choices.text: Ask for time to pay

effects.log: She enters that, with the interest. The Ancestor has all the time there is, and you do not.

events.text: A debtor in the hills has died owing, and the debt falls to whoever will take it up. It falls, this time, to you, if you want your gate. Ran has written out the name, and she has very neat handwriting, and you did not know them at all.

choices.text: Take the debt onto your page

effects.log: It joins the rest, in red. You think about them sometimes, the stranger whose years you are now paying off. Nobody else does. The gate opens.

choices.text: Leave it for someone else

effects.log: Someone else takes it, and somebody else's gate opens. Yours can wait.

events.text: The blight has got into the rice at Lower Sang, and they have a bad winter coming. You could carry them through it. It would cost you more than you would like and they will not be grateful for long. Headwoman Ahn has sent word only to tell you the price of grain, and nothing else.

choices.text: Buy the grain, and carry it up yourself

effects.log: All winter, on your own back as often as not. They grumble about the quality, and they live. In the spring there is a very small cake at your gate, and your gate is open.

choices.text: Send a part, and call it enough

effects.log: It is a good deal, in truth. Some of them do well on it. The cake goes to somebody else.

events.text: A flood at the Ferry Quarter, and Ferryman Tu is sitting on his roof with eleven other people and a goat. Everyone has been told help is coming. Nobody has said from where. You have no boat, and a very good idea of what the wharf will charge you.

choices.text: Hire every boat on the wharf

effects.log: The wharf makes a fortune. So does Tu, in a way: he has become a kind of hero, and he tells it as if he rowed you. The goat survives. The gate opens.

choices.text: Hire one boat, and go yourself

effects.log: You get Tu and the goat. You see the other roofs from the boat. You do what you can, and it is not this gate's price.

events.text: A great sum, paid out in the open. You stand at the head of the Silk Bridge at noon with the ledger and the chests, and you settle up with every person your house has ever short-changed, whether or not they knew. A crowd has gathered. Comptroller Sim is reading out the names, with relish.

choices.text: Pay every name, down to the last

effects.log: It takes until dark. It is a very great sum. By evening your name in this province is good for rather more than you have just spent, and Sim is doing the arithmetic on that, delighted.

choices.text: Pay the great names, and send clerks to the rest

effects.log: It is noted that you did. It is noted, with figures, in the same book.

events.text: You have bought up the debts of a whole river town, on purpose, and today you mean to do something with them. The town has come out to see what. Clerk Yu has written a speech, which is a mistake. It is your account, and the gate is watching how you close it.

choices.text: Close it at one coin a family, in public

effects.log: They pay, in a long line, a coin each, each with a receipt. It is the strangest day the town has ever had. They name something after you, slightly wrong. The account is closed.

choices.text: Hold on to the paper a little longer

effects.log: It is excellent paper. It goes on paying. The gate, like any creditor, will wait.

events.text: You take out the list at last. The next name is a tax-farmer called Do, who ruined a family long ago, and you have let him live to be fat. He is at home today. It would take one visit. Gyo has marked the page, without comment.

choices.text: Go to Do, and make him pay what he owes

effects.log: You sit in his very fine front room until he has counted it out, and written out what he did, and signed. It takes a day. You strike his name. The gate opens, without much joy.

choices.text: Next year: he is not going anywhere

effects.log: He is not. Neither is the gate.

events.text: A name from the old page has turned up in Hanam, running a school. You had thought them dead. They are very good with the children, you are told, and very frightened, and they have started to expect you. They have stopped locking the door.

choices.text: Go, and name the price to their face

effects.log: You sit on one of the tiny school benches. They agree to every word of it. They ask if they might finish the term. You strike the name, the last week of the term.

choices.text: Let them wait a while longer

effects.log: It costs nothing, this kind of waiting, and they will go on doing it. The gate does as well.

events.text: A carter at the foot of the temple road swore at you this morning, for nothing, and you have been polishing your answer ever since. It is an extremely good answer. It is nearly noon. You sit down by the road with it, as you were told to, and wait to see which of you gets bored.

choices.text: Sit until the answer has gone

effects.log: It goes around the time the carter comes back the other way. He nods. You nod. You could not now tell anyone what it was you were going to say.

choices.text: Go and find the carter

effects.log: You find him, and you deliver it. It is as good as you thought. The gate has not moved.

events.text: You are spoken of now, and that is the trouble: young monks stop talking when you come in. Elder Beopjin sends you down to the leper village at Goksan for the winter, where nobody has heard of you, and hands you a bucket. Someone there has already told you to mind where you put it.

choices.text: Carry the bucket until spring

effects.log: They call you "you there" the whole winter. An old woman with no fingers teaches you a song about turnips. When you climb the temple road again, the quiet you came for has been following you for some time.

choices.text: Send a junior with your good wishes

effects.log: The junior does very well. You hear about it. The gate does not seem to have been told.

events.text: The man who killed your oldest friend has become a monk at a small temple in the south, and the abbot there writes to say he is dying, and asks if you will come. You have not been angry about this in thirty years. You have told a great many people so. You notice that you have read the letter four times.

choices.text: Go, and sit with him

effects.log: He does not ask for anything. Neither do you. You hold the cup for him on the last evening, since nobody else is there, and on the road home you find the place in you where that anger lived has only a draught in it.

choices.text: Send a kind letter

effects.log: It is a very kind letter. Your hand is quite steady. You read it four times before you send it.

events.text: Your own disciple has been struck by a drunk lord at the ferry, in front of a crowd, for not getting out of the way. Half the temple is watching to see what you will do. You could end that lord with a look from here. You go down to the ferry and the anger comes with you, in step, like an old friend.

choices.text: Ask the lord to tea, and hear him out

effects.log: It is the longest cup of tea of your life. He is a very unhappy person. He sends an apology after a week, and rice after a month, and your anger walks home a little behind you, sulking.

choices.text: Let the lord feel your eyes on him, just once

effects.log: He falls off his horse. Nobody can say you did anything. You know how much that was worth.

events.text: Nobody in the murim can make you angry now, and pilgrims say so. So you go to the one place left: the old hut where you grew up, and the grave with the name you have never said in any hall. You have crossed oceans of qi to avoid this little hill. It has started to rain.

choices.text: Sit by the grave until you can say the name

effects.log: It takes eleven days. You say it, in the end, in a voice you have not used since you were small. Nobody hears. The rain goes on, and the great gate in you opens with no sound at all.

choices.text: Bow from the road, and go on

effects.log: It is a very correct bow. There is a good deal of hill left between you and it.

events.text: The gate above this one will take you past anything a person has ever been angry about. You find, on the morning you sit down to it, one thing left: you are rather pleased with how calm you have become. It is a very small thing. It is looking at you, from the middle of your chest, with great contentment.

choices.text: Sit with that as well

effects.log: It is much the hardest of them. It lasts a year. It takes a novice asking you if you are the one who sweeps, and you saying yes, and meaning nothing by it.

choices.text: Decide that this one is harmless

effects.log: It agrees with you entirely. It goes on looking very pleased.

events.text: There is a bend in the river below the temple where the water does something you cannot explain, and Old Yeon Cheol has been asking you about it since you were a child. You were told to take a season. You bring a stool, which he confiscates. You sit down on the bank, on the ground, and start to look at it.

choices.text: Stay until you stop trying to explain it

effects.log: In the eighth week a leaf goes round it twice and you laugh out loud, and you could not say why. Yeon Cheol, from a long way off, seems to have heard.

choices.text: Write down a theory, and go home

effects.log: It is a very sound theory. The water goes on doing what it was doing.

events.text: Your name has reached the capital. There are people on the mountain path now, looking for you, with gifts. So you go further up, past the goats and the last shrine, to the ledge where an old hermit once lived. They left a bowl there. It has been empty for sixty years, and it is a very good bowl.

choices.text: Stay until they stop coming

effects.log: It takes two years. By the end the path has grown over, and you have started to put out water for the crows. No one in the capital can quite remember what they wanted you for.

choices.text: Come down and send them away politely

effects.log: You do it well. Next spring there are more of them, with better gifts.

events.text: You have a fine sword, the finest you have ever held, and it has been with you through everything. There is nothing wrong with it. You stand on the bridge over the deep pool for a whole afternoon, wondering why you have brought it here, and you know quite well why you have brought it here.

choices.text: Let it go, and walk on empty-handed

effects.log: It makes hardly a sound. You feel foolish all the way to the far bank, then lighter, then nothing in particular. A year later somebody asks what became of your sword, and you have to think.

choices.text: Carry it home again

effects.log: It is a very fine sword. It fits your hand as well as it ever did.

events.text: A war is coming through the valley below your mountain, and from up here you can see exactly how you could stop it. It would take one afternoon, and it would be your doing. The whole of your training says that things go better when you do not. You have never believed that less than you do this evening.

choices.text: Stay on the mountain, and watch all of it

effects.log: You watch all of it. It stops by itself, at the river, for reasons nobody could have planned. You will never know if you were right. That turns out to be what this gate wanted to know about you.

choices.text: Go down, just this once

effects.log: You go down, and you do some good. The mountain is exactly where you left it, and so is the gate.

events.text: You can no longer remember the last time you were cold. Old friends have died. The goatherd Ji's great-grandchildren bring you cheese without knowing your name. A season alone means nothing at this height, so you try the other thing: you go and sit in the busiest market in the province, as nobody, with a bowl.

choices.text: Sit there until nobody sees you

effects.log: They step round you for a year. A child draws on your knee with a stick. You have stopped being alone, and you have stopped being with anybody, and one morning you notice it is all the same mountain.

choices.text: Stay until someone recognises you

effects.log: A scholar does, in the third month. You are very gracious about it.

events.text: At the top of the mountain, at the end of everything you ever learned, there is a small flat stone. You have sat on it for many years. Today you notice that you have started thinking of it as your stone. It is a very slight thought. Way off down the valley, a goat calls.

choices.text: Get up, and leave the stone

effects.log: You go down the far side, where you have never been, without a stick. There is a path there, as it happens. There has always been a path. You are not sure anyone is walking on it.

choices.text: Sit a little longer

effects.log: It is a very good stone. It will still be good tomorrow.

events.text: A widow has been coming to your office every month for six years about a boundary stone, and every clerk you have knows to tell her you are out. It is about eleven feet of bad land. You find out this morning that you have been out for six years. She is waiting on the bench, with her lunch.

choices.text: Walk the boundary with her yourself

effects.log: It takes a day and a very muddy pair of shoes. She was right, by about nine feet. You sign the correction there in the field, on your own back, with her holding the ink.

choices.text: Have a clerk look into it, properly this time

effects.log: A clerk does. There will be a report. She finishes her lunch.

events.text: You are an important person now, and the job has got easier for it, and that is what is wrong. You ask to be sent for a year to the worst county on the list. The prefect thinks you are joking. Nobody has held the post at Lower Mok for more than eight months, and the last man left at night.

choices.text: Go, and stay the year

effects.log: The roof leaks, the clerks steal, and there is a feud in the tax rolls four generations old. You come back grey. Lower Mok has its first honest ledger in living memory, and it hates you, and it pays its taxes.

choices.text: Send a good deputy with your full support

effects.log: He is a very good deputy. He leaves at night in the seventh month.

events.text: Your own son-in-law, or someone who might as well be, has been caught with a hand in the granary: a junior you raised up, who owes everything to you. The rule requires you to be the one who hears the case, or to step aside and say why in writing. Everyone at your table is being very careful with the soup.

choices.text: Hear it yourself, by the book, in open court

effects.log: You read out the sentence in your usual voice. It is the law, it is not the worst the law allows, and you do not soften it by one word. You also go and see them every month.

choices.text: Step aside, and let another hand do it

effects.log: It is entirely proper. You explain why in writing. You have rather good handwriting.

events.text: There is an order from above on your desk, correct in every form, that you know to be wrong. It will move four villages for a canal that will never carry a boat. You can carry it out. Or you can write a memorial saying so, under your own name, to people who can end your career with one stroke.

choices.text: Write the memorial, and sign it

effects.log: You write it plainly, and you send a copy to the archive, so it cannot be mislaid. You are demoted three grades by return of post. The canal is quietly dropped, four years later, by someone else.

choices.text: Carry it out as gently as it can be done

effects.log: You do it very gently indeed. There is a small shrine to you in the new village. You do not go there.

events.text: Young officials quote you now, some of them correctly. You are asked to write the preface to the new examination manual, the one every student in the empire will copy out. It would be very easy to say what they would like you to say. Tutor Hwang Sun is long dead, and you can still feel the tutor reading over your shoulder.

choices.text: Write down what the job really is

effects.log: It runs to one page. It says what it costs. The Board of Rites has it softened twice, and you have it put back twice, and it goes out. Forty years later, a magistrate you never met quotes it on a flooded road.

choices.text: Write something fine and safe

effects.log: It is very fine. It will be copied out by a million hands. Not one will slope.

events.text: You have held the highest office open to you, for longer than most people live. At this gate the Rites ask for a last thing: who will do this after you, and have you made them able to tell you that you are wrong? You call in the brightest of them. They have brought a very careful report on your successes.

choices.text: Ask for the other report

effects.log: It takes them a month to believe you. Then they bring it, shaking. It is forty pages. They have you on the salt tax, and they are right. You sign it, and you put them in your chair, and you go home.

choices.text: Thank them for the report you have

effects.log: It is an excellent report. It is entered in the record, with your name.

events.text: The Iron Banner Escort has been passing off a bad debt onto a boy of sixteen, who signed something he could not read, and the whole of Plum Ford knows and is sorry about it. The Escort has eleven swords in town. You are not known here yet. You are having a very nice lunch, and you put down your chopsticks.

choices.text: Go over to their table

effects.log: It costs you a tooth and most of your lunch money. The paper goes in the fire. By the time you are out of town, you have a name in Plum Ford, and you have started to find out what those weigh.

choices.text: Leave the boy some money, quietly

effects.log: It is more than he has ever seen. He is very grateful. The Escort takes it from him by morning.

events.text: A great house has invited you to its feast, and it is a real honour, and the head of it is going to announce an alliance over the wine with a man you know sold out the Ma's Landing militia. You have no proof that a court would hear. You have your seat at the high table, and your name.

choices.text: Stand up at the toast, and say it

effects.log: You say it, in nine words, and you stay on your feet while the room looks at you. You are not asked anywhere for a long time. In the spring, three people you have never met write to you with the proof.

choices.text: Have a quiet word with the head afterwards

effects.log: They hear you out, very courteously. The alliance goes through. You were not at the toast, in the sense that matters.

events.text: Your oldest enemy has been cornered by forty men at Dry Well, none of them honest, and a boy has come to you with the news, thinking you will be pleased. You are, for about a breath. You have fought that person for twenty years, in the open, by the rules. These people are not going to use the rules.

choices.text: Go and stand next to them

effects.log: It is a very odd afternoon, back to back. When it is over they look at you, bleeding, with absolute loathing. "Why," they say. You tell them you have not finished with them yet. It is told all over the south.

choices.text: Let it happen

effects.log: It happens. You hear they did not go easily. Nobody will ever blame you, and you have no one left to fight.

events.text: They want to give you a title. It is a real one, from the Alliance, with a seal. All you have to do is stand on the dais next to a very great man while he says he has always been your friend. He has not. A good many people who stood under your flag are buried because of what he did, and were never named.

choices.text: Stand on the dais, and name them

effects.log: You take the seal, you read out forty-one names, and you put it back on the table. It takes some time. Nobody on the dais moves. It is the only speech from that day that anyone can remember.

choices.text: Take the title, and do some good with it

effects.log: You do a great deal of good with it. It is a very heavy seal, for its size.

events.text: You are very nearly a legend now, and a legend can do no wrong: there is the trouble. A young swordsman has challenged you, fairly, at the Red Ford, and has told everyone you are past it. You could end the matter by not turning up. Nobody would think less of you. The challenge is a little insulting. They are also, you hear, very good.

choices.text: Go, and let them have their real fight

effects.log: They are very good. You do not hold back, because they asked you not to. They lose, and they go home with something better than what they came for. So, a bit, do you: you were nearly past it.

choices.text: Send a kind word, and a gift

effects.log: It is a very gracious gift. They hang it up where everyone can see it, and they do not say what they think.

events.text: The whole murim would follow you now, if you told it to, and you have just been told something that would cost you all of it: the great victory your name rests on, at the Last Pass, was won by someone else, who died on the rock, and whose name nobody wrote down. You are the last one alive who knows.

choices.text: Say so, in the open, where you are seen

effects.log: You say it on the anniversary, at the pass, to all of them. There is a very long silence. Somebody starts a bad song, with a new name in it. You find you can stand up straighter without all that on your back.

choices.text: Let it lie. It would do no one any good

effects.log: It would do no one any good. You go on being thanked, and it goes on being true.

events.text: A wagon boss on the Ford Road has a dog the size of a calf, and two sons the size of the dog, and he has been telling people in the inns that the road is his now. You are not sure it is yours to dispute. You have a sore shoulder. On the other hand, you did ask for this.

choices.text: Go and tell him otherwise

effects.log: The dog is the worst of it. You lose a sleeve, and you win the road, for now, and the two sons help carry you in. The dog comes and sits next to you, having changed its opinion.

choices.text: Wait until your shoulder is better

effects.log: It gets better. The sign on the road has his name on it by then.

events.text: A sect has moved its gate down onto the Heron Road, a proper sect, with robes, and sixty disciples who have been told that the rule of the road is a thing of the past. You have been told that too, in a very nice letter. You are big enough now that it is an insult to send only a few.

choices.text: Walk up to their gate alone

effects.log: They send out their best, one at a time, as they were taught, which is very polite of them. By evening their master comes out himself. By morning there is a toll on their gate. They pay it with great dignity.

choices.text: Send someone stronger than the letter

effects.log: Your lieutenant does it. They are very impressed by your lieutenant, who has begun to notice.

events.text: You have got large, and comfortable, and nobody has tried you in six years, and you are beginning to believe that is on account of your strength. A girl who sells eels has told you to your face that you have gone soft. Her eels are not very good. You find you cannot stop thinking about it.

choices.text: Go out alone on the wild roads, with no name

effects.log: For a year you are nobody. You lose twice. You win a mule. It is the best year you have had since you were nineteen. You bring the eel-seller a very large fish, and she says it is not very good.

choices.text: Have the eel-seller moved along

effects.log: She is moved along. Nobody has told you that you have gone soft since.

events.text: There is a thing up in the Black Pines that has eaten three hunting parties and one small sect. Nobody has seen it and lived to describe it. It is not on any road. It pays no toll. You have been told about it many times, in a tone that says nobody expects you to do anything about it.

choices.text: Go up there, and see

effects.log: You do not ever quite describe it. You come down in nine days, with a scar and a very large tooth. People stop you in the road to ask, and you find you have stopped wanting to tell them.

choices.text: Put a toll on the road around it

effects.log: It is a very clever toll. People do pay. Up in the pines, something goes on eating.

events.text: Nobody below the clouds can stop you now. You have looked. You have gone out and looked, for years. So at this gate you do the one thing left that you could lose: you go and find the person who beat you first, when you were young, who is old now, and very frail, and you ask to be taught what they did.

choices.text: Kneel, and ask

effects.log: It is the hardest thing you have taken from anyone. They laugh for some time, and they make you carry water. On the fortieth day they show you, with one finger. It is very simple. You go home a good deal stronger, and a little quieter.

choices.text: Send them a very fine gift

effects.log: They send it back with a note. It says "Still?"

events.text: You are told that nothing under heaven can fight you. So you go up on the roof of the stronghold in the worst storm in forty years, and take off your coat, and stand up to it. It is not a metaphor. It is a very large storm. It has no idea who you are. All the roads you ever taxed are running with water.

choices.text: Stay up there until one of you stops

effects.log: It goes on for three days. You lose. It does not notice. When the sun comes up, you are sitting on the wet tiles, laughing, with every bone in you singing, and you are not anywhere near the top of anything, and that is such a relief.

choices.text: Go in, you have made your point

effects.log: You go in. Your people are very impressed. The storm did not ask.

events.text: There is a ferry family at Willow Steps with a sick grandfather, and they have already sold the boat. The apothecary has told them the truth, which is the price. It is not so large a price, to you. Suri has stopped looking at your purse, and that is how you know that she has been looking at it.

choices.text: Pay, and do the needle work yourself

effects.log: The old man is back to shouting at the river by the new moon. They buy the boat back, and they try to pay you in carp. You take one carp, as is proper.

choices.text: Show them which weed will ease it

effects.log: It eases him. It is a good weed. They bury him in the autumn, and they send you some carp.

events.text: The salt-miners at Heuksan have a lung sickness that everyone knows about and nobody will treat, because the mine owner pays the physicians. He has quite a lot of money. He has offered you a retainer as well, on hearing you were in the district. Your own cure for it would take every jar you own and most of a year.

choices.text: Spend the year, and every jar

effects.log: You set up in a shed. The owner sends men, and you are polite to them, as to anyone at your fire. By spring half the shift is breathing, and the mine has to pay more to keep them. You are out of jars.

choices.text: Take his money, and treat them in secret

effects.log: It is a very clever arrangement. It lasts until he finds out, which he has known all along.

events.text: A plague pit of a town has been shut up by the army at Seoha, and it is in your own province, and the fever in it is a thing nobody has seen. The only one who could do the work is at your table: you. You could send your best student. She is ready. She is also twenty-two.

choices.text: Go yourself, and keep her out

effects.log: You go in with a list of what you do not know. It gets shorter. You come out in the fourth month, thinner, with the cure in your own handwriting and the marks of it on your neck. She will not speak to you for a year, for going without her.

choices.text: Send her, with all you have

effects.log: She does splendidly. You would like everyone to know that. You check the road each morning.

events.text: You have made a cure, the finest of your life, for a wasting sickness of the rich. A prince offers you a fortune to keep the recipe secret and sell it by the dose. Aunt Dok, long dead, did exactly this, you have recently found out. It paid for your whole education. You sit up with the two sets of accounts.

choices.text: Give the recipe to every physician in the province

effects.log: You have it copied out four hundred times, at your own cost. The price of it falls to nothing in a year. The prince sends you a very cold letter. You put it with the accounts.

choices.text: Sell it, and use the money for cures

effects.log: You use all of it for cures. Everyone agrees it is a good arrangement. You look at the dose-price, some nights.

events.text: They bring you someone at the end of everything, and it is a poison of your own, one you made in your bitter years, for money, that was supposed to be without a cure. You did not think any of it was left. You have never tried to cure it. You know exactly why. You sit down with what is left of the patient, and clear the table.

choices.text: Find the cure, whatever it takes

effects.log: It takes all you ever learned, and two years, and you have to try it on yourself first. It works. You write it out, and burn the other recipe. One more thing in the world has its cure, as you once swore.

choices.text: Make them comfortable

effects.log: You are extremely good at that. They do not suffer at all. You keep the old recipe in its box.

events.text: At the top of the art there is one poison left to study: the thing that kills everyone in the end, and has no second jar. You have put it off for some centuries. Your needle-girl's great-grandchild asks you what it is you do all night. You have a very long list of what you would need, and it would use up the rest of what you own.

choices.text: Spend it all on the study, and give the findings away

effects.log: You do not find it. Nobody will. But you find eleven things on the way, and your name is not on any of them. Old people in the south live a little longer now, and do not know why, and the jars are all empty.

choices.text: Keep a little by, for later

effects.log: It is a sensible amount. There is, after all, a good deal of later.

events.text: The Red Clerk's price this time is small, and it is told to you in the corridor. There is a friend you write to. There is a name you sign those letters with, and only they use it. It is to be given up: you will sign the other name from now on. "That is all?" you ask. He looks at you with what may be pity.

choices.text: Sign the other name

effects.log: They write back, puzzled. Then they stop asking. You read it over, at the lamp. You are quite surprised, some months later, by how much of you was living in that one word.

choices.text: Write once more with the old name, and leave the Clerk waiting

effects.log: It is a very good letter. The Clerk knows when it went.

events.text: You have a name in the Mountains now, and the Clerk's prices are told in the Hall of Lamps. This time it is a thing you are proud of: the time you spared someone, when you were young and everyone said you should not. You will go to the record room and strike it out, in your own hand. It will be as if you had never done it.

choices.text: Strike it out

effects.log: One line. In the morning you go to remember why you did it, out of habit, and find an ordinary room with nothing in it. The person, somewhere, is still alive. It will not be told who they were.

choices.text: Leave that page alone

effects.log: The Clerk nods, and turns his lamp down. It will be asked again, in a smaller voice.

events.text: There is a village that has paid the Cult for three generations and has never been any trouble. A dark price is told to you, in one line: it is to stop being protected. You need not do anything at all. You need only take your name off the page, and it will all be told, in time, to you.

choices.text: Take your name off the page

effects.log: You take it off. You do not go near that road for many years. Nobody blames you, as nobody has been told. It is told in the hall in nine words, and you have stopped counting them.

choices.text: Keep your name there another year

effects.log: The village keeps paying. A hall master asks after your health, in a certain tone.

events.text: You have a student, and the student loves you, in the way students do. It has made you weak in a very particular place, and the Clerk has noticed, with his usual interest. The price is that they must learn what you are. You are to tell them yourself. You are to leave nothing out. You choose the evening.

choices.text: Tell them all of it

effects.log: They listen right to the end. It is a very quiet room. They bow, they go, and they are a much more dangerous person after that, and they never again turn their back on you. It is told, and it is entered.

choices.text: Find another way to pay

effects.log: The Clerk does not have another way. He will wait. Your student brings you tea.

events.text: You could take the throne of the Mountains now, and everyone knows it, so at this gate the price is told by the old Lamp Elder himself, who has been expecting it. It is your own name, your first one, the one on no page. Once it goes, nobody living or dead will ever have called you by it. It is a very small thing, for what it opens.

choices.text: Give it to him

effects.log: He writes it on a slip, and holds the slip to the lamp. You watch it go. You leave the hall and you stop on the stairs, trying to work out why you stopped. You stand there for some time. Nobody dares ask.

choices.text: Tell him that it is not for sale

effects.log: He looks almost pleased. "Everything is," he says, kindly. "Come back when you know the price."

events.text: There is nothing left to pay with. The Clerk has gone through the whole book with you, and it has taken a season. He closes it at last and sits back, and for the first time in your whole life he looks tired. "One thing," he says. "You could stop wanting anything from it." The whole hall of lamps is burning very straight.

choices.text: Stop

effects.log: It is told in no words at all. The lamps do not flicker. You walk out past the Clerk, and he stands up. Nobody has seen him stand before. There is nothing at all in you that a dark price could be paid out of, and that was the price.

choices.text: Ask him what you would get for it

effects.log: He laughs, and it is an awful sound, and he opens the book again at the first page.

events.text: Your first great payment. Ledger Sister Ran reads out the figure: the first ten good harvests of your life, or so the reckoning has it. You do not know what that means. You sign. On your way out, you notice you can no longer call to mind the smell of cut hay, which you are almost certain you once liked.

choices.text: Let it be entered

effects.log: It goes down in red. You will smell it again, some day, in a field, and you will think only that somebody is cutting hay. The gate opens.

choices.text: Ask for the figure to be read again

effects.log: She reads it again, more slowly. There is a small fee for that.

events.text: You are important enough now to carry a debt for others. Ran lays out the account of a small sect in the hills, who fell behind, and are very frightened. You may take their page onto yours, or the Collectors will go up there. It is told that the Ancestor does not care which. There are forty of them, and you have seen the children.

choices.text: Take their page onto yours

effects.log: It is a very long page. You feel it in your back on the stairs. They will never know. You are not sure that is a mercy, or what the Ancestor will think you are up to. It is entered.

choices.text: Let the Collectors go up

effects.log: They go up. It is told, in a few words, and you sign that you have been told.

events.text: Old Debtor Bae has died at last, at a great age. It turns out that he left you something, in a very neat hand: forty years of what he owed, along with the duck's great-granddaughter. It is the first time that anyone has ever willed a debt to you out of affection. Sister Ran seems to find it interesting.

choices.text: Accept the whole of it

effects.log: You do. The duck is not grateful. You take its page as well, in a manner of speaking. On certain evenings you find you are sitting on Bae's old step, thinking about nothing, and the book seems a bit lighter for no reason anyone could enter.

choices.text: Pay off the duck, and leave the rest

effects.log: It is entered at the value of one duck. Ran does not smile. She never has.

events.text: The deep hall has asked for you by name, which it has never done. Sister Ran ties the red cord on you with her own hands and does not meet your eye. The figure is not told. You are told only that what you carry down will not come up again, and that you may choose what to carry.

choices.text: Choose the thing you would least like to lose

effects.log: It will not be told here. You carry it down the stairs in both hands. You come up the stairs with both hands empty, and you keep looking at them. The cord is taut. It is entered as paid in full.

choices.text: Choose something else

effects.log: You choose something else. It is accepted. Ran looks at you, and adds a very small note.

events.text: You have paid so much that the figures have started to go the other way. Ran shows you this, frowning. The Ancestor, it seems, now owes a little to you. Nobody has ever seen this before, and there is no column for it. There are a number of frightened people in the corridor. You could call it in. You could let it stand.

choices.text: Let it stand, and pay on

effects.log: You pay on. Nobody understands it. Ran rules a new column, by hand, and writes nothing in it. You think you can feel something, far below, stop looking at the page and start looking at you.

choices.text: Call it in

effects.log: You call it in. Nothing happens for a very long time. Then the book is shut, and it opens at a fresh page, with the old figure at the top.

events.text: The last payment is told to you by no one. You find it written at the foot of your page, in your own hand, and you do not remember writing it. It says that every breath you have ever drawn was on loan, and it asks you to return one. Just one, the first one. Sister Ran, very old now, is holding the cord.

choices.text: Breathe out

effects.log: It is a very long breath. Nobody can say afterward how long. Ran rules off the page, ties it up in red, and for the first time in all her years she closes the book and sits with her hands in her lap.

choices.text: Hold on to it

effects.log: You hold on. You are very good at that. So is the book.

events.text: The two bad bridges were only the start. Now it is the Lower Sang road, washed out, and the village cannot get its rice to market. Headwoman Ahn tells you what it will cost, and gives you a look at your shoes. The people of the hall are all very busy, and they have been busy since she came up the hill.

choices.text: Pay for the road, and carry the first stone

effects.log: It takes all the spring. Your disciples stop being busy when they see you with the stone. The rice goes down to market in the autumn. Ahn says that the bend is too sharp.

choices.text: Send silver, and a promise to look in

effects.log: They build it themselves, in the end, and rather well. It does not go past your gate.

events.text: A whole county has come to you now, since word has got round: nine thousand people, and a magistrate who has run away. You did not ask for it. You are not a government. You have a hall and some good intentions, and the first frost was last night. They have begun to sit down in your yard, very politely.

choices.text: Feed them, and find out who can run a kitchen

effects.log: You find forty people who can. It is the most frightening winter of your life and you never once know what you are doing. In the spring the county goes home, and they leave you a very great many cooking pots.

choices.text: Send them on to the prefect, with provisions

effects.log: It is good sense. They go, with your provisions. You watch them all the way down the road.

events.text: The tax has been lifted, thanks to you, and the great families of the province are furious. They would like a word. It turns out that you have made yourself the person who stands between them and the people, and it is a very exposed place to stand. You could buy them off with something small. It would only be one village's water rights.

choices.text: Spend your own silver, and give up nothing of theirs

effects.log: It costs a fortune, and it goes on costing it. The water stays where it is. The families do not love you. You had not expected that a thing could be so expensive and so dull.

choices.text: Give up the water rights, for the greater good

effects.log: It is, very nearly, for the greater good. There is a village you ride around now.

events.text: Someone in Ahn's village has done a terrible thing, one of the people you swore for, and there is a crowd. The crowd is very like the one you have fed for twenty years. It knows your face. It would like you to look the other way for an hour. Ahn's daughter, grey now, has come up the hill to say what she thinks you should do.

choices.text: Stand in the door, against the people you swore to

effects.log: You stand in the door all night. They do not hate you for long. They do hate you. In the morning there is a trial, slow and fair, and nobody is ever really happy about it, and it goes in the village records.

choices.text: Go inside, and let them

effects.log: It is over in an hour. They bring you rice the next day, as always. You do not know what to do with your hands.

events.text: They have built you a temple. You did not ask for it. Old women in five provinces burn incense to you for good harvests, and you have started getting the requests. It is a very great many requests. Your hall could run on the offerings for a century. Somewhere near the coast, a child has been named after you.

choices.text: Knock it down, and put a granary on the footings

effects.log: It is very unpopular. Several old women tell you what they think of you, to your face, and it is the best thing you have heard in years. The granary is full by autumn. They burn the incense there, and you have stopped arguing.

choices.text: Let it stand: it gives people heart

effects.log: It does. It gives them a great deal of heart. It takes in rather more than it gives out.

events.text: A hundred years of bad winters, and you have carried a good many of them. Everyone you knew at the beginning is gone. Now you must do what no one wants you to: teach them all to manage without you. You could keep on saving them. They would like it. You could go on for a thousand years, and they would never learn what a granary is for.

choices.text: Hand it all over, and go

effects.log: It is badly done, at first. There is a hard year, and you stay away, and it is the worst thing you have ever done. They manage. Nobody in the valley remembers why the road has that very sharp bend.

choices.text: One more winter

effects.log: There is always one more winter. They are very glad to see you.

events.text: Clerk Yu has found that your hall has never paid its cooks what the books say that it pays them, not once, going back to before you came. It is a small sum, compared to anything. It is rather a large sum, to a cook. Bok-nam is at the back door now, gutting fish, and does not know yet.

choices.text: Pay it all back, with the interest, in the kitchen, in person

effects.log: You count it out on the chopping board. Bok-nam looks at it for a long time, then at you, and goes on gutting fish. There is a very good dinner that night. The account is closed.

choices.text: Raise their wages from now on

effects.log: It is a handsome rise. Everybody is very pleased. The old column is still there, if anyone looks.

events.text: The whole province now keeps its accounts in your paper. One word from you would make a town rich, or break it. A delegation from Hanam has come to ask what you mean to do about the rice price this year, in the voice people use for weather. Comptroller Sim has noticed that a person could do rather well here.

choices.text: Publish your books, and your plans, for anyone to read

effects.log: Nobody has ever done such a thing. It costs you a fortune in lost advantage. Sim is in mourning. By next year nobody in the province is afraid of the rice price, and they all pay their debts to you on time.

choices.text: Set a fair price, and keep your books shut

effects.log: It is a very fair price. They thank you. They go on using that voice.

events.text: A great bank has failed in the south, and it is not your fault at all. Twenty thousand people held its paper. It is no business of yours. Everything is paid for, you swore, and every debt is written down. Those debts have your rival's name on them. You could buy them all, for a song, this week, and be repaid in names for a hundred years.

choices.text: Buy it all, and honour it at full face

effects.log: It very nearly breaks you. Sim has to lie down. But there is not a shop in the south that will not take your name on a scrap of paper now, and there will not be for a hundred years.

choices.text: Buy it at the market price, and collect

effects.log: It is the deal of the century. It is also entirely legal. They pay you, slowly, and teach their children your name.

events.text: You have grown old enough to have paid for some bad things. Sim, also old, has brought a thin file, without being asked. It is every person who has died of a debt to your house, in forty years. It is not as thin as it looks. There is a column for what they owed, and a blank one beside it, ruled by Sim.

choices.text: Fill in the blank column, and pay it to whoever is left

effects.log: It takes two years to trace them. It is a very great sum. Nobody can tell you what it buys. You sign the last line. Sim takes the file back, and for once does not say what it comes to.

choices.text: Thank Sim, and put it on the shelf

effects.log: It is a very tidy file. It goes with the others. Sim makes a note of where.

events.text: The Emperor would like a loan. It is the largest sum anyone has ever asked for. It would buy a war. Every other house in the empire would give anything to be in your place, and the terms are excellent, and you know precisely how many people that sum comes to, since you are the one person alive who has done the arithmetic.

choices.text: Refuse, in writing, and show your working

effects.log: It is the most dangerous letter ever sent by a private person. You send the arithmetic along with it. There is a very long silence from the capital. The war does not happen that year. You keep a horse ready.

choices.text: Lend it, at the excellent terms

effects.log: It is repaid in full, with interest, on the day. It is the best-kept account in your whole house.

events.text: Nothing under heaven is unpriced to you any more, and that is the last account. You sit down with Sim, who has outlived all reason, to close your own: what you were given for nothing, what you never paid for, and to whom it is owed. Your mentor's patience. The rain. It is a long list, and there is no one to pay.

choices.text: Pay it anyway: give it all away, at no price, and close the book

effects.log: You give it all away. It takes a year, and it causes a good deal of trouble. Sim writes "closed" across the last page, and blots it, and then, very carefully, smiles. There is a great silence where the arithmetic used to be.

choices.text: Enter it as a bad debt

effects.log: It is the correct entry. It is the only bad debt you have ever carried. It is also the largest.

events.text: A name from near the top of the list, and an easy one: a petty clerk, who once falsified one small paper that started all of it. You had forgotten him. List-Keeper Gyo has not. He is seventy now, and he sells ink. He sold you some, a year ago, and gave you the right change. Gyo has already sharpened a pen.

choices.text: Go and buy some ink, and tell him the price

effects.log: He knew you at once. He has been expecting it for thirty years. He writes it all out, in his good hand, for the family, and takes it to them himself. You strike the name. It was very good ink.

choices.text: He is hardly worth it. Next year

effects.log: He sells you some more ink, next year. He gives you the right change.

events.text: You are strong enough now to do what you said you would do to the Bang family, all of them, and they know. They have sent you their youngest, a girl of nine, with a letter, as a sort of hostage or apology. She has very carefully washed her face. Your book does not have her name in it. It does have her family's.

choices.text: Send her home, then go to the elders and collect

effects.log: She goes home with an escort. You go up to the Bang hall, in the open, and you read out what is owed, and who by, and they pay it, every line, with the elders looking at the floor. Her name was never on the page.

choices.text: Keep her, as security, and write them a list

effects.log: It is an extremely effective letter. She is very well treated. She is learning to read by looking at your book.

events.text: One of your own has taken a name from your list and gone out and settled it without you: badly, and in your name, and with a good deal of harm to people who were not on any page. It is the boy Nam, grown. He has come back, shining. He is waiting for you to say well done. Gyo has opened the book and is holding out the pen.

choices.text: Enter it, under your own name, and go and pay for it

effects.log: You write it in. You go down there yourself, with Nam walking behind you, and you stand in front of each of them, and you pay. He stops shining around the second house. You did not forgive it for nothing.

choices.text: Strike the name. It is done, after all

effects.log: It is done, after all. Nam is very happy. Somebody down there has started a book of their own.

events.text: Word has come up that the person you have hated longest is dying, in a great bed, in a great house, surrounded by many grandchildren, of nothing but years. It is very nearly too late. You could be there in nine days, and it would be the worst thing that has ever happened at a deathbed. The list has one thing to say on this.

choices.text: Go, and collect it at the bedside, quietly, from them alone

effects.log: You send the grandchildren out. It takes one afternoon. They know what they did; they have always known. They say it, in the end, in a small dry voice, and you write it down and you sign it. You stay till it is over. You could not tell anyone why.

choices.text: Let them die in peace, and leave the name

effects.log: They die in peace. The name is on your page, in ink. There is nobody to send the bill to now.

events.text: You have struck every name on the first page, and most of the second. People tremble. You open the book one evening to the back, where Gyo keeps the entries of what was done by you and yours, over all these years, in that very clean hand. You had not known that part of the book was so long. There are a lot of children on your list who have grown up.

choices.text: Start at the top, and go and see them

effects.log: You go on foot, with no escort, and you tell each one who you are and what you owe. Two try to kill you. One is very kind, which is worse. It takes nine years. Gyo rules off one column for every one.

choices.text: Close the book for the evening

effects.log: It closes very easily. Gyo has oiled the binding. It has a good, heavy sound.

events.text: There is one name left. It is at the very top of the very first page, above the one you began with, and you have never read it, because you wrote it there when you were young, and you know whose it is. It is yours, for not having been there, on the day it all started. Gyo holds out the pen and looks away, out of courtesy.

choices.text: Name your own price, and pay it, and strike it

effects.log: It costs you the list. All of it: the whole book goes in the fire, with Gyo feeding it page by page. Nothing is owed to you now under heaven. You are very cold for a while. Then someone asks what you would like for dinner, and you have no idea.

choices.text: Turn to the next page

effects.log: There is always a next page. Your hand is very steady. Gyo takes up the pen again.

events.text: The bell at the temple does not ring. It has never rung on such an occasion: that is rather the point. Elder Beopjin sends you your bowl, wrapped in a clean cloth, by a novice who has been told not to speak.

effects.log: It is a comfortable thought, and you have it for some time. The oath, for its part, has not changed its mind about anything.

events.text: Elder Beopjin hears you out, on the long stairs, with a broom. "Take that one," the elder says. "We shall see." They mean all thousand and eighty, every day, for as long as it takes, and they mean it very kindly.

choices.text: Sweep until they stop watching

effects.log: A year goes by. One morning there is a bowl beside the broom, in its old place in the row. Nobody says anything. It is the kindest thing that has ever happened to you.

choices.text: Leave the broom against the wall

effects.log: It is still there when you look back. It will be there.

events.text: Old Yeon Cheol sees you coming up the path, and goes on feeding the goats. "You yielded to the wrong thing," he says. "It happens. Water does it too. You would know the way back better than me."

choices.text: Give up what you took for it, and go up alone

effects.log: You leave it at the bottom of the mountain with your name on it. A season later you are sitting by the stream, and at some point the leaf you brought has floated off.

choices.text: Tell him you only came to see how he was

effects.log: He looks well. He says so. You go down the way you came.

events.text: Registrar Gu has the book open at your line. "One took a bribe, one told a lie, one was me," the registrar says. "It takes about nine years, and I have written out the first of them." The list is on very good paper.

choices.text: Take the list, and confess in writing to whom it names

effects.log: Every one of them gets a letter, signed. Some write back. It costs you a great many friends, and a very great deal of pride, and then one day the registrar writes a new line under the red.

choices.text: Ask if the list could be shorter

effects.log: The registrar sharpens a pen and says it could be longer.

events.text: You find Old Banner Cheon by the mending frame, with the flag across his knees. He has a good many needles, and he does not look up. "Hold this end," he says. It is what he always said, to everyone. It does not mean anything has been decided.

choices.text: Hold it, and stand where you are seen, as long as it takes

effects.log: For a year you stand at every fight the house has, in front, with no rank. People stop asking why. One morning he hands you the hem without looking up, and you take it.

choices.text: Say you came to explain

effects.log: He hears all of it, with a needle in his mouth, and bites off the thread.

events.text: Toll-Mother Gang's successor has you up to the roof, and hears you, chewing. "It is a very short law," they say. "You can get back under it. You go out and you take something, from someone stronger, in front of everyone. And you do not do it the way you did the last thing."

choices.text: Go and find someone stronger, and do it in the open

effects.log: It costs you three teeth. It is told on every road by the new moon, and on the Heron Road they stop holding out the tolls. Big Deok looks you in the eye again.

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: They spit over the wall. There is no hurry, as far as the road is concerned.

events.text: Aunt Dok is older. She has you sit down at her fire, and looks at you for a while. "You know what a poison is," she says. "You know what the cure is. Tell me what you did, and I will tell you what it costs." Suri stands in the door, grown now, and says nothing.

choices.text: Tell her, and make the cure, at your own cost

effects.log: It is a harder thing to make than the thing you did. It takes a season and all you have, and she checks every leaf. At the end she gives back the needle, and she says it is still only the second-best.

choices.text: Tell her most of it

effects.log: She nods, and looks at her hands. "Most," she says. She gets up to see to the fire.

events.text: The Red Clerk has your page open. "It can be mended," he says, with a kind of distant interest. "It has been done. It wants proof that you are not soft after all, or proof that you always were and it did you no harm. I have seen both. I have no preference."

choices.text: Pay the price he names, told to nobody

effects.log: It is not set down here. He rules a line. A lamp is carried back up the hall, to where the air is still. You stand and look at it, and you are not at all sure what it was you bought.

choices.text: Ask him what he would do

effects.log: He looks at you for the first time ever. "Nobody has asked," he says, and closes the book, and leaves you there.

events.text: Sister Ran takes your page down from the shelf and unties the cord with very neat fingers. "The arrears," she says, and turns it around. It is a great many lines. "The Ancestor will accept instalments. The Ancestor has never yet refused a payment. Nor has the Ancestor ever yet forgotten a missed one."

choices.text: Pay the arrears

effects.log: You feel each one go. It takes a long time. She rules it off at the end, and ties a new cord, and your hands are yours again, and you are older than you were.

choices.text: Say you need another season

effects.log: She enters that. It goes on the bottom of the page, with interest.

events.text: Headwoman Ahn gives you a bucket, and shows you the charcoal mark on your gate, which is still there after all this time. "You can wash that off," she says, "when somebody else asks you to." She nods down the hill, toward a great many doors you will have to go and knock at.

choices.text: Knock on all of them, and do what they ask

effects.log: It is mostly roofs. One year and nine villages. Somebody small, whose name you have forgotten, comes up the hill with a rag in the spring, and starts on the mark without asking.

choices.text: Wash it off now, it is your gate

effects.log: It comes off easily. It is back, very neatly, by morning.

events.text: Comptroller Sim sets the three copies on the table and taps the clause you wrote yourself. It is a dreadful sum. Sim thought so at the time. "It is entirely enforceable," says Sim. "I do not believe anyone has ever actually paid one before. I should be most interested to see it."

choices.text: Pay the clause in full, and have it witnessed

effects.log: It takes a very long time to count. Sim watches every coin. At the end the three copies are burned in a dish, and Sim does something with their face which might, in another person, be a smile.

choices.text: Offer to settle for half

effects.log: Sim makes a note of the offer, for the file. It is a very thick file.

events.text: List-Keeper Gyo turns to the page with your name on it. "None is forgiven for nothing," the keeper says. "You wrote that. So. What are you going to pay, and who to?" The boy Nam, grown now, is sitting by the door with his hands on his knees.

choices.text: Name your own price, a hard one, and pay it in front of Nam

effects.log: It takes as long as it takes. When it is done, Gyo holds out the pen, and it is Nam who strikes the name. He does not say it is forgiven. He says it is paid. You will take that.

choices.text: Ask whether it might be enough to be sorry

effects.log: Gyo writes that down too, under the name, for the record.

effects.log: You give your word, at the table. {npc} thanks you and pays for your supper, which is a thing you will think about later.

choices.text: Say it is yours now, and step outside

ok.log: It is over before the soup is cold. {npc} sits up in the road, bows from there, and says that the temple will be sorry to hear it.

fail.log: {npc} folds you up like laundry, without hurting anything that matters. {He} sits with you till you can stand. "Please think about it," {he} says.

choices.text: Make an offering to the temple for what it taught you

effects.log: It is a very great offering. {npc} counts nothing, and writes you a receipt in a beautiful hand.

events.text: {npc} is waiting on the bridge, in very clean sandals, with a staff. "You were asked," {he} says. {He} does not raise {his} voice. Behind {him}, a small group of novices has come along to learn something.

choices.text: Meet {him} on the bridge

ok.log: {npc} goes into the river, rather neatly. The novices fish {him} out. {He} bows to you, dripping, and goes home to report.

fail.log: You come to on the bank, with a poultice on. It is a very good poultice. The novices have left you some rice.

choices.text: Go round by the ford

ok.log: You get wet, and you are away before the novices have stopped staring.

fail.log: They are at the ford too. They are very patient. You get across with a staff-shaped bruise.

events.text: {npc} comes back to see how your meridians are doing, with a basket of herbs and a look of real concern. {He} is, you realise, quite sincerely sorry, and quite prepared to do it again. Whoever did this to you can undo it.

choices.text: Make {him} undo it

ok.log: It takes all night and most of the herbs. {npc} works on you without being asked twice, murmuring the whole time.

fail.log: {He} takes your pulse afterwards and shakes {his} head. "Another year," {he} says, and leaves you the basket.

choices.text: Take the basket, and send {him} home

effects.log: {npc} bows. The herbs are good, though they are not what you need.

events.text: A novice arrives with a letter, and stands on one foot while you read it. The temple has sent all the people it can spare, and it wishes you well. It adds that it will go on praying for you, and that you are to understand this as a threat.

choices.text: Keep it somewhere you can see it

effects.log: You keep it. It is a strange thing to be proud of. You find that you still fight rather better for knowing nobody is coming.

choices.text: Throw it away, and go on

effects.log: It goes in the fire. You fight with what you fight with, and nobody comes, and it is very quiet. You had not realised how much you listened for them.

events.text: You find {npc} sitting on your wall one morning, swinging {his} feet. Nobody saw {him} come. "That thing you do with your left wrist," {he} says, pleasantly. "We would like it back. I do not know how, either. It is a very odd request. Could you stop doing it, perhaps?"

choices.text: Say you will stop

effects.log: {npc} seems delighted, and climbs down off the wall the wrong way, and is gone. You check, and all your chickens are still there.

choices.text: Knock {him} off the wall

ok.log: It takes three tries, and {he} seems to think it is a very good game. {He} waves from the road.

fail.log: There is nothing to hit, and then there is a hand on your neck. "Oh, dear," {npc} says. "I am so sorry. Sit down a moment."

choices.text: Send the mountain a large gift for its roof

effects.log: {npc} weighs it in {his} hand. "They will hate that," {he} says, delighted. "Yes. That should do it."

events.text: {npc} is standing in the middle of a river, on the water, fishing. "They sent me again," {he} calls out. "I did tell them." {He} puts the rod down, looking a bit embarrassed for both of you, and there is no sound as {he} starts to walk toward you.

choices.text: Meet {him} on the bank

ok.log: For an hour neither of you lands anything. Then you do. {npc} lies on the bank laughing at the sky. "Oh, that was good," {he} says. "I will tell them it was terrible."

fail.log: You lose track of where you are, somewhat, and then you are sitting in the water. {npc} has gone back to fishing, and offers you one.

choices.text: Leave, without any hurry

ok.log: You stroll away. {npc} watches you go, and approves, and it is a little insulting.

fail.log: {npc} has somehow got there first. You leave with a wet sleeve and a sense of being humoured.

events.text: {npc} has come to look at what they did to you, and {he} clicks {his} tongue. "Clumsy. I said so. They should have sent me." {He} rolls {his} sleeves up, and then looks at you, thoughtfully. "Of course, I would have to be made to."

choices.text: Make {him}

ok.log: It is the oddest fight you have had. At the end of it your meridians are running clear, and neither of you could say exactly when that happened.

fail.log: "Not yet," {npc} says, patting your head, and strolls off. "You are still pushing."

choices.text: Tell {him} you will find a physician

effects.log: "Very sensible," {npc} says, and looks disappointed.

events.text: A pressed leaf arrives, tied to a goat. The mountain has decided that what you carry off will wear away by itself, as things do. It is not angry, and it will not send anybody else. You keep the goat.

events.text: {npc} presents {his} card at your door, and a document in triplicate. It is a formal notice that a certain art was taught under terms, and you are using it in breach of them. {He} would be very grateful for your signature, here, and here. {He} also happens to have a very long sword, tucked neatly out of the way.

choices.text: Sign, and undertake to stop

effects.log: {npc} blots it, thanks you, and leaves your copy on the table. It is the politest defeat of your life.

choices.text: Tear it up, and see about the sword

ok.log: It is a very correct fight. {He} salutes before and after. {He} makes a note of the result, and asks you how to spell your name.

fail.log: The sword is as correct as the document. You are politely disarmed. {npc} makes a note of that too, and sets your arm for you.

choices.text: Pay the fee in the document's last clause

effects.log: It is a large fee. {npc} writes a receipt, then a receipt for the receipt, and bows.

events.text: Your second notice arrives by hand, {npc}'s hand, at the crossroads, in front of witnesses {he} has thoughtfully brought along. "You were served," {he} says, "on the date shown." The sword comes out very straight. One of the witnesses has started to take notes.

choices.text: Answer the notice

ok.log: It is entered in the record that {npc} lost. {He} corrects the witness's spelling from the ground.

fail.log: It is entered in the record that you lost. A copy will be sent. A physician is also sent, at your expense.

choices.text: Go out by the side road

ok.log: You go. Witnesses note the time. A letter of complaint gets to your door ahead of you.

fail.log: There is a witness on the side road. It costs you a fall, a long explanation and some dignity.

events.text: {npc} comes round with a formal review of your condition, as the regulations provide. A remedy can be ordered, {he} explains, if the sanction was excessive. Only the sanctioning officer can order it, and that is {him}, and {he} sees no reason to, unless compelled.

choices.text: Compel {him}

ok.log: {He} writes out the order for your treatment with one hand, while holding {his} ribs with the other. It is very legible.

fail.log: The review is closed for this year. {He} leaves you a form.

choices.text: Say you will appeal to the prefect

effects.log: {npc} thinks that is an excellent idea, and tells you the fee.

events.text: A final notice arrives, very thick. The house has weighed the cost of pursuing you against the worth of the art. It finds the matter closed, and regrets that it ever opened it. It would be obliged if you would not mention this. A receipt is enclosed.

events.text: {npc} rides up in broad daylight, by the front gate, with the house colours on, and gets down and waits for you to come out, as is proper. "You know why I am here," {he} says. "That art was taught under the banner. If you are done with the banner, then be done. Put it down. I would rather not make this about steel."

choices.text: Give your word to put it down

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long moment, then takes your word, as {he} takes everyone's, without a witness. {He} rides away. You are not sure you could look at {him} and break it.

choices.text: Tell {him} to get {his} sword out

ok.log: A straight, loud, honest fight. {npc} gets up laughing, with a split eyebrow, and shakes your hand before {he} leaves.

fail.log: {npc} puts you on your back, and helps you up, and brushes off your coat. "I will tell them you fought well," {he} says. "You did. Think about it."

choices.text: Pay the house for what it gave you

effects.log: {npc} is embarrassed by the money, and takes it anyway. "It will go to the widows," {he} says.

events.text: {npc} has come back, and has brought only {his} sword, and has told everybody in town when and where. There is a crowd now, and a man selling chestnuts. "I said I would rather not," {he} calls out. "You know how this goes."

choices.text: Walk out to meet {him}

ok.log: The crowd has its money's worth. {npc} yields, and says so, loudly, so nobody can say otherwise. Someone buys you both a chestnut.

fail.log: Everyone sees you go down. {npc} stands over you only long enough to see you breathing, and then {he} turns round to tell them not to cheer.

choices.text: Go over the back wall

ok.log: You are over and away. It is not a thing anyone will forget, and they are all telling it by nightfall.

fail.log: The back wall is high, and you are not as young as you were. You do get over it, though the fall is witnessed.

events.text: {npc} has heard what they did to you, and it was not done by {his} leave. {He} is here to say so, to your face. "There is a way to undo it," {he} says. "I will show you. But you will have to take it from me, in the open. I do not give things to deserters."

choices.text: Take it from {him}

ok.log: It is the hardest you have ever been hit by someone who wanted you to win. {npc} shows you the way of it, after. Your meridians run clean again.

fail.log: "Not today," {npc} says, helping you up. "Come again. I will still be here."

choices.text: Thank {him}, and refuse

effects.log: {npc} nods. It is a very respectful nod, and it makes you feel rather worse.

events.text: The house sends one last rider, unarmed, and the rider reads it out in the road. The banner has sent enough of its friends to you, and it will send no more. It does not forgive you. It only remembers how you fought. You find you stand up straighter to hear it.

events.text: {npc} steps out from behind a tree, picking {his} teeth, with five friends. "That trick of yours," {he} says. "That was the stronghold's trick. You owe for that. You can pay, or stop doing it, or we can talk about it now, I do not mind." {He} genuinely does not. {He} sounds a bit hopeful.

choices.text: Say you will stop

effects.log: {npc} looks disappointed, and tells you so at some length. {He} also takes your hat.

choices.text: Talk about it now

ok.log: When it is over, {npc} is lying under the tree, grinning with what is left. "That was nice," {he} says. "They will send someone else now."

fail.log: You wake up without your hat, your boots or your good opinion of yourself. There is a small note that says "think about it," and you would like to know who taught {him} to write.

choices.text: Pay the road its toll, in full

effects.log: {npc} counts it twice, licking {his} thumb. "That is the first time anyone has ever done that," {he} says, slightly shaken.

events.text: Your dinner is interrupted by {npc} coming through the wall of the inn, where there was not previously a door. {He} seems pleased. "You were told," {he} says, shaking off bits of the wall. "Nobody ever listens. It is the best part of the job."

choices.text: Put {him} back through it

ok.log: The innkeeper is very upset. {npc} is carried off by {his} friends, singing. You leave a good deal of silver on the table for the wall.

fail.log: You go through the other wall. The inn is having a very bad evening. {npc} takes your dinner, and eats it over you.

choices.text: Out of the window, fast

ok.log: You are off down the road before the dust settles. Somewhere behind you, {npc} has started to laugh.

fail.log: You land on one of the friends, who is waiting there. It is not a good landing, for either of you.

events.text: {npc} turns up to see if what was done to you has taken. {He} pokes your chest with a finger, like someone testing a melon. "Some can be un-done, you know," {he} says. "There is a knack. I could be persuaded. The road has only ever had the one way of persuading anybody."

choices.text: Persuade {him}

ok.log: {He} shows you the knack, with a broken nose, in a very good mood. It hurts as much coming out as it did going in. You run clean.

fail.log: "Nope," {npc} says, from above you. "Not persuaded." {He} seems sorry about it.

choices.text: Tell {him} to go and find a melon

effects.log: {npc} shrugs, and goes. It is a long road, and {he} knows where you live.

events.text: Someone leaves a boot on your step, with a coin in it. That is how the road says so: it has stopped being worth anybody's time. You have been written off, as a loss, by people who do not write. Nobody on the Heron Road will take your toll now, and it almost feels like respect.

We would like you to stop using our art, in the open, where people can see how it is done. Do say yes. I so dislike it when I have to come twice."
events.arc: What the Bitter Root Wants Back

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: {npc} finishes {his} tea, tips the server, and goes. You do not drink anything else that day, or, to be honest, that month.

choices.text: Throw the tea at {him}, and draw

ok.log: You win, somehow, on a stomach that is beginning to have doubts. {npc} leaves you an antidote on the way out, "as a formality."

fail.log: You fall over the table. It was not the tea. It was the handle of the cup. {npc} leaves a cure, and tells you what it would have been otherwise.

choices.text: Buy the art outright, with a very large purse

effects.log: {npc} tastes a coin, with interest. "They said you would," {he} says. "Enjoy your tea."

events.text: {npc} has come to the market where you are, with very clean hands and gloves on over them. "A second visit," {he} says, in a tone of regret. "I do so hate them." The stallholders near you are starting to find reasons to go and have lunch.
events.arc: What the Bitter Root Wants Back

choices.text: Get in close, before {he} can use those

ok.log: You get in close. It is a nasty, itchy sort of win. {npc} sits down on a crate, and starts calmly working out how many hours you have, and hands you the jar.

fail.log: You never see the needle. You spend three days seeing a good many things, and on the fourth you wake up, with the antidote on your chest and a bill.

choices.text: Leave by the rooftops, breathing through your sleeve

ok.log: You are gone, and only your sleeve has gone a slightly odd colour.

fail.log: It was on the roof tiles. You get away, in the sense that you do go somewhere, and you are ill for a week.

events.text: {npc} visits to look at your tongue and pull down your eyelid. {He} is pleased with the work. "There is a cure," {he} says. "There is always a cure, it is the first thing we teach. It is on me, in fact, in this sleeve. All you would have to do is take it."
events.arc: What the Bitter Root Wants Back

choices.text: Take it

ok.log: You get the sleeve. It is the cure, along with a good many things which are not. You pick your way through them with shaking fingers. {npc} watches and gives you a mark out of ten.

fail.log: You get the wrong sleeve, and you lose another week. {He} leaves a note saying which sleeve it was.

choices.text: Say you will make your own

effects.log: {npc} is honestly delighted. "Do write to me how it goes," {he} says.

events.text: A small jar arrives by a very nervous carrier. It is honey, and only honey, and you have it tested four times. The house says that you are no longer worth the good needles. In its way that is a sort of peace. Your food tastes of food again, some days.

"You took a thing from the Mountains," {he} says, without any heat. "You use it where people see it. It is bad for the price. Stop, and this is the last you will see of me. I am told that I am very restful, as a last sight."
events.arc: What the Red Ink Wants Back

choices.text: Say you will stop

effects.log: {npc} nods. The lamp starts to flicker in the wind like a normal lamp. When you look up, the chair is just a chair.

choices.text: Put the lamp out in {his} face

ok.log: It is a hard thing to win against someone who is not at all bothered. You manage it. {npc} gets up, pulls down {his} sleeves, and makes a note.

fail.log: You find you have been lying on the floor for a while. {npc} is reading your letters. "Next time," {he} says, without looking up.

choices.text: Pay what the Cult asks for it

effects.log: The number is told to you in one line. You pay it. {He} gives you a receipt in red ink, and it does not dry.

events.text: The whole street has gone dark but for one lamp, and {npc} is holding it. "Twice," {he} says. {He} says it as though that is a remarkable number. People behind their shutters are being extremely quiet. Up at the end of the street, somebody is shutting the city gate.
events.arc: What the Red Ink Wants Back

choices.text: Walk up the street

ok.log: One lamp goes out. In a little while, the others on the street come on, one at a time. {npc} is not there any more. There is a small scorch on the stones.

fail.log: It is morning when you wake, in a ditch outside the gate, with your purse still on you. That is the message, you understand: they do not need your purse.

choices.text: Go over the roofs, away from the lamp

ok.log: You get out, and you do not stop for two days. The lamps follow you for one of them.

fail.log: The roofs have lamps too, as it turns out. You get out, but not cleanly.

events.text: {npc} comes to look at the hollow place they left in you, with professional interest. "It can be filled," {he} says. "You would have to reach into me and get it. Most people are too frightened of what else is in there." {He} opens {his} hands.
events.arc: What the Red Ink Wants Back

choices.text: Reach in

ok.log: You will not tell anyone what else is in there. You get what is yours. The hollow place closes, and {npc} sits down rather suddenly, and for the first time {he} looks at you with something like respect.

fail.log: You let go at the last moment. {npc} shuts {his} hands. "Next year," {he} says. "Same offer."

choices.text: Keep your hands to yourself

effects.log: {npc} nods as if that was the clever answer, and is gone.

events.text: A page comes under your door in the night, in old red ink, with your name on it and a line ruled through. The Cult no longer considers you worth a lamp. You have never been so insulted, and you sleep very well.
events.arc: What the Red Ink Wants Back
